title: Waakye with Shito
summary: Ghana's favourite breakfast: rice and black-eyed peas cooked together in water stained deep red by dried sorghum leaves, served with shito, a dark pepper oil fried slowly with dried fish and shrimp, and boiled eggs. It is here because it teaches cooking a legume and a grain in one pot so both finish together, and because shito is a sauce whose whole character comes from frying patiently until the oil runs clear.
skills: rice and beans coloured with sorghum leaves
shito, a slow-fried pepper and dried fish oil
equipment: Large heavy pot with a tight lid
Heavy saucepan or deep frying pan for the shito
Clean glass jar with a lid for storing shito

ingredients.note: rinsed until the water runs clear
plus boiling water for topping up

ingredients.item: Smoked dried herring or other smoked dried fish
Gari (toasted cassava granules) and fried ripe plantain

mise: Soak the peas overnight in plenty of cold water.
Rinse the waakye leaves and tear any long ones in half.
Rinse the rice in several changes of water until clear and drain.
Blend the onions, garlic and ginger with 2 tbsp (30 ml) water to a smooth paste.
Grind the dried shrimp and the dried fish separately to fine powders.

timeline.do: Make the shito; it keeps for weeks.
Boil the leaves to colour the water.
Simmer the peas until soft.
Add the rice, boil, then steam on low.
Boil the eggs; fry plantain if using.
Fork the waakye and serve with shito and eggs.

steps.do: Make the shito. Heat the oil in the heavy pan over medium heat and add the onion, garlic and ginger paste. Fry, stirring every few minutes, for about 25 minutes until the water has cooked away and the paste turns golden.
steps.look: The paste spits at first, then sizzles quietly as the water goes, and smells sweet and toasted.
steps.mistake: Rushing on high heat, so the paste burns at the bottom while it is still wet on top.
steps.fix: Keep it at medium to medium-low and scrape the base often. Burnt specks make it bitter; if it scorches badly, start again.

steps.do: Stir in the tomato purée and fry 5 minutes, then add the ground shrimp, ground fish, chilli powder and stock cube. Lower the heat and fry for 20 to 30 minutes more, stirring often.
steps.look: The mixture darkens to a deep brick red and then almost black-brown, and the oil separates clearly and sits on top. It smells deeply savoury and smoky.
steps.mistake: Stopping when it is merely red, which leaves a raw, gritty taste that spoils quickly.
steps.fix: Keep frying until the oil runs clear on top; that is both the flavour and what helps it keep.

steps.do: Cool the shito completely and spoon it into the clean jar, making sure the oil covers the top.
steps.look: A dark, glossy, gritty paste under a layer of red oil.
steps.mistake: Using a wet spoon or jar, which shortens its life.
steps.fix: Keep it in the fridge and always use a clean, dry spoon.

steps.do: For the waakye, bring the 6 cups (1.4 litres) water to the boil with the leaves and bicarbonate and boil 10 minutes, then lift the leaves out.
steps.look: The water turns a deep mahogany red within minutes.
steps.mistake: Adding more bicarbonate for a deeper colour, which makes the rice slimy and soapy.
steps.fix: Never more than 1/4 tsp (1 g). Darker colour comes from more leaves, not more alkali.

steps.do: Add the drained peas and simmer with the lid ajar for 30 to 40 minutes, topping up with boiling water so they stay covered.
steps.look: A pea crushes to paste between finger and thumb while its skin stays whole.
steps.mistake: Adding the rice while the peas are still firm, so they never catch up.
steps.fix: Peas first, always. Test several; they must be soft before the rice goes in.

steps.do: Stir in the rice and salt. The liquid should sit about 1 inch (2.5 cm) above the rice; add boiling water or ladle some out as needed. Boil uncovered over medium-high heat until small craters appear across the surface and most of the water has gone, about 8 minutes.
steps.look: Steam holes appear all over and the surface looks like it has tiny volcanoes.
steps.mistake: Too much water, which gives a mushy pot.
steps.fix: If it looks soupy, keep boiling uncovered a few more minutes before covering.

steps.do: Cover tightly, turn to the lowest heat and leave 15 to 20 minutes without lifting the lid. Then rest off the heat 10 minutes.
steps.look: When you tilt the pot no water pools at the base, and the grains are tender with no hard centre.
steps.mistake: Lifting the lid and stirring, which breaks the rice.
steps.fix: If the rice is still firm, sprinkle 3 tbsp (45 ml) boiling water over, cover and leave 10 minutes more.

steps.do: Meanwhile boil the eggs 9 minutes, cool in cold water and peel.
steps.look: Firm whites, set golden yolks.
steps.mistake: Leaving eggs in hot water, which gives a green ring round the yolk.
steps.fix: Cool them in cold water straight away.

steps.do: Fork through the waakye gently to lift the peas and separate the grains. Serve with a spoonful of shito, a halved egg and gari or plantain alongside.
steps.look: Rust-red rice studded with peas, glistening dark shito, white and yellow egg.
steps.mistake: Stirring with a spoon, which mashes the peas.
steps.fix: Use a fork and lift from the bottom.

science: The colour comes from red pigments in the dried sorghum leaves, close relatives of the anthocyanins in red cabbage. Like them, they change shade with acidity: in neutral to slightly alkaline water they turn deep red-brown, which is why a pinch of bicarbonate deepens the shade. The same alkali loosens pectin in the pea skins so they soften faster. Too much alkali breaks down the rice starch surface into slime and tastes soapy. Shito works by frying water out of the paste. As moisture leaves, the temperature in the pan climbs well above boiling, and the sugars and proteins in onion, shrimp and fish brown deeply. Once the water has gone, the oil separates, and the low moisture, together with salt and chilli, is what lets shito keep.
plating: A generous mound of waakye on a plate or, in the Accra way, on a banana leaf, a spoonful of shito on top or beside it, a halved boiled egg, a pile of gari and a few slices of fried plantain. Add a little stewed tomato sauce if you have it.

pairing.drink: A cold sobolo, the Ghanaian hibiscus and ginger drink, whose tart, spiced edge balances the rich shito.

variations: Add a stewed tomato and meat sauce, as the street vendors do.
Without waakye leaves, the dish tastes the same but stays pale; a few dried hibiscus flowers boiled briefly give some colour.
Make the shito milder with half the chilli and a little sweet paprika.
safety: Shito spits as the paste fries; use a deep pan and long sleeves, and stir with a long wooden spoon.
Keep shito in the fridge under its oil and use a dry spoon each time.
Cooked rice should be cooled and refrigerated within 2 hours; rice left warm can grow harmful bacteria.

title: Masala Dosa
summary: A thin, crisp crêpe made from a fermented batter of rice and urad dal, folded round a spiced potato filling and served with coconut chutney. skills: soaking and grinding rice and urad dal
spreading thin on a hot griddle
equipment: Large bowl with room for the batter to double
Cast-iron dosa tawa or wide nonstick frying pan, 11 to 12 inch (28 to 30 cm)
Flat ladle or a 1/2 cup (120 ml) measure with a round base
Half an onion on a fork, for oiling the pan

ingredients.note: boiled in their skins until tender

ingredients.item: Fresh or frozen grated coconut, for the chutney
Roasted chana dal (dalia) or roasted peanuts
Green chilli and ginger, for the chutney

mise: Rinse the rice three times and soak in plenty of water. Rinse the urad dal with the fenugreek and soak separately. Soak both for 6 hours.
Boil the potatoes in their skins, cool, peel and break into rough chunks.
Slice the onion, chop chillies and ginger, pick the curry leaves.
Blend the coconut, roasted dal, chilli, ginger and a pinch of salt with water to a thick chutney; temper with mustard seeds and curry leaves fried in oil.

timeline.do: Soak the rice and dal.
Grind and leave to ferment overnight.
Check the batter, salt it, make the filling and chutney.
Heat and season the tawa.
Cook the dosas one at a time.
Fill, fold, serve hot.

steps.do: Drain the urad dal and fenugreek and blend with about 1/2 cup (120 ml) cold water for 4 to 5 minutes, adding water a spoonful at a time, until very smooth and fluffy. Scrape into the large bowl.
steps.look: A pale, light, airy batter, almost like whipped cream, that slides off a spoon in soft folds.
steps.mistake: Grinding with too much water, giving a thin batter that does not trap gas.
steps.fix: Add water slowly; stop when it is fluffy. Cold water keeps the blender from heating it.

steps.do: Drain the rice and blend with about 3/4 cup (180 ml) water until it feels like fine semolina when rubbed between your fingers. Mix it thoroughly into the dal batter with your hand for 2 minutes.
steps.look: A thick batter like pancake batter, with a very faint grit.
steps.mistake: Grinding the rice completely smooth, which gives a softer, less crisp dosa.
steps.fix: A slight grain is right; it gives crispness.

steps.do: Cover loosely and leave in a warm place, ideally 80 to 90°F (27 to 32°C), for 8 to 14 hours. An oven with only the light on works well.
steps.look: The batter rises to nearly double, is full of small bubbles, smells pleasantly sour and yeasty, and is lighter in texture.
steps.mistake: A cold kitchen, where it barely rises and the dosas come out flat and pale.
steps.fix: Give it longer, or put it in the oven with the light on. Cold batter can take 24 hours.

steps.do: Stir the batter gently, add the salt, and loosen with water a spoonful at a time until it pours like double cream.
steps.look: It flows easily off the ladle in a thick ribbon and settles flat.
steps.mistake: Making it thin like milk, so it breaks and leaves holes on the tawa.
steps.fix: Add water slowly; if too thin, stir in a spoonful of rice flour.

steps.do: Make the filling. Heat the oil in the saucepan over medium heat, add the mustard seeds and chana dal and fry until the seeds pop, then the curry leaves, chilli and ginger for 30 seconds, then the onion for 5 minutes until soft. Add turmeric, salt, the potatoes and 1/4 cup (60 ml) water. Crush lightly and cook 3 minutes.
steps.look: Popping mustard seeds, a burst of curry leaf aroma, then a golden, chunky, moist potato mixture.
steps.mistake: Adding the curry leaves before the seeds pop, so the spices never bloom.
steps.fix: Wait for the seeds to crackle; that sound is your cue.

steps.do: Heat the tawa over medium-high heat for 5 minutes. Rub it with the cut onion dipped in a little oil. Spray or sprinkle a few drops of water on the surface.
steps.look: The water drops dance and evaporate in about 2 seconds.
steps.mistake: Spreading on a pan that is too hot, so the batter sets before you can spread it, or too cool, so it sticks.
steps.fix: If the water vanishes instantly, lower the heat a little; if it lies and simmers, wait longer.

steps.do: Pour a ladle of batter, about 1/3 cup (80 ml), into the centre. Immediately, using the base of the ladle, spread it in a continuous spiral outwards, pressing lightly, to a round about 10 inches (25 cm) across.
steps.look: A thin, even, lacy round with tiny holes appearing as it sets.
steps.mistake: Stopping and starting, which leaves thick ridges.
steps.fix: Use one fluid motion. Your first two or three will be imperfect; that is normal.

steps.do: Drizzle 1 tsp (5 ml) ghee round the edge and over the surface. Cook without turning for 2 to 3 minutes over medium heat.
steps.look: The edges lift from the pan and curl, the underside turns deep golden and crisp, and the top looks dry.
steps.mistake: Removing it too soon while the base is pale and soft.
steps.fix: Wait for real colour underneath; lift an edge to check.

steps.do: Spoon a line of filling across the centre and roll or fold the dosa into a cylinder or a triangle. Serve at once. Wipe the tawa with the onion and sprinkle water before each new dosa to cool it slightly.
steps.look: A crackling golden crêpe round a soft yellow filling.
steps.mistake: Pouring the next dosa onto a pan that is now too hot.
steps.fix: The water sprinkle and onion rub bring the pan back to the right heat.

science: The batter is fermented by wild lactic acid bacteria and yeasts present on the dal, rice and your hands. They feed on sugars and produce lactic acid, which gives the tang, and carbon dioxide, which leavens the batter. Urad dal matters because its proteins and its sticky, gum-like carbohydrates form a stretchy network that traps those bubbles. Fenugreek helps the fermentation along and adds aroma. On a very hot griddle, the thin layer of batter loses water almost at once, the starch sets and the sugars brown quickly, which is why a thin spread gives a crisp dosa. Salt is added after fermenting because it slows the microbes. Mustard seeds release their flavour only when they pop in hot oil.
plating: A long oval platter or banana leaf: the dosa folded into a long cylinder or a cone, crisp side out, a small bowl of coconut chutney and one of sambar beside it. Serve each dosa straight from the pan; they soften within minutes.

pairing.drink: South Indian filter coffee, strong and milky, whose roasted bitterness balances the sour batter and spice.
pairing.brennans: New Orleans-Style Coffee with Chicory: like many South Indian filter coffees, the house coffee is blended with chicory, a link worth mentioning to a coffee-curious guest.

variations: Plain dosa: no filling, served with chutney and sambar.
Mysore masala dosa: spread a thin red chutney of chilli and garlic inside before adding the filling.
Uttapam: pour the batter thick and top with onion, tomato and chilli for a soft pancake.
safety: The tawa is very hot; keep the handle turned in and use a dry cloth or glove.
Fermented batter keeps 3 to 4 days in the fridge; discard it if it smells unpleasantly sharp or shows mould.

title: Jian Bing
summary: Northern China's street breakfast: a thin mung bean and wheat crêpe with an egg cooked straight onto it, painted with bean sauce and chilli, wrapped round a shattering fried cracker and herbs. It is here because it is a crêpe built in layers at speed, a lesson in heat control and timing, and because it brings deep frying into the crêpe lesson.
skills: a mung bean and wheat batter
cracking an egg on the crêpe
equipment: Large nonstick frying pan, 12 inch (30 cm), or a flat griddle
Ladle and an offset spatula or wide fish slice
Deep heavy saucepan for frying the crackers

ingredients.item: Sweet bean sauce (tianmianjiang) or more hoisin

mise: Whisk the flours, five-spice and salt, then whisk in the water to a smooth batter as thin as single cream. Rest 15 minutes.
Mix the hoisin, bean sauce and 1 tbsp (15 ml) water into a paintable sauce.
Slice the spring onions, chop the coriander.
Crack each egg into its own cup.
Set up the frying station: oil in the deep pan, thermometer, spider, rack.

timeline.do: Mix the batter and rest it.
Fry the wonton crackers.
Heat the crêpe pan.
Cook the crêpes one at a time, about 2 minutes each.
Fold and eat at once.

steps.do: Heat the oil to 350°F (175°C). Fry the wonton wrappers two at a time for 30 to 45 seconds, turning once, until puffed and golden. Drain on the rack.
steps.look: The wrappers bubble and blister instantly and turn light gold; they shatter when broken.
steps.mistake: Oil too cool, giving greasy, chewy crackers.
steps.fix: Check the thermometer between batches and let the oil recover.

steps.do: Heat the large pan over medium heat for 3 minutes and wipe it with a thin film of oil using kitchen paper.
steps.look: A drop of batter sets in about 5 seconds without browning fast.
steps.mistake: A pan too hot, so the batter sets in lumps before it spreads.
steps.fix: Lower the heat; wipe with a damp cloth to cool quickly if needed.

steps.do: Pour in a ladle of batter, about 1/3 cup (80 ml), and immediately spread it thin with the bottom of the ladle or by tilting the pan, to a round about 11 inches (28 cm).
steps.look: A thin, even, matte sheet that sets within 30 seconds.
steps.mistake: A thick crêpe that will not fold.
steps.fix: Use less batter next time and spread faster.

steps.do: Crack an egg onto the crêpe, break the yolk with the spatula and spread it across the whole surface. Scatter spring onion, coriander and sesame seeds over the wet egg.
steps.look: A thin layer of egg covering the crêpe, herbs and seeds sticking to it.
steps.mistake: Leaving the egg in a lump, which cooks unevenly.
steps.fix: Spread it right to the edges quickly while it is still liquid.

steps.do: When the egg has set, about 45 seconds, loosen the edges with the spatula and flip the whole crêpe over.
steps.look: The egg side is set and lightly golden; the crêpe lifts cleanly.
steps.mistake: Flipping too early, so egg sticks to the pan.
steps.fix: Wait until the egg looks matte, then slide the spatula all the way under before turning.

steps.do: Brush the top, the crêpe side, with about 1 tbsp (15 ml) of the bean sauce mixture and a little chilli oil, then scatter zha cai if using.
steps.look: A thin, even, glossy dark layer.
steps.mistake: Too much sauce, which makes it soggy and slips out.
steps.fix: A thin coat is enough; the flavour is strong.

steps.do: Lay two crackers in the centre. Fold the left and right sides over them, then fold in half and slide out of the pan.
steps.look: A neat rectangular parcel, slightly crisp outside, with a crunchy centre.
steps.mistake: Waiting before eating, so the crackers soften.
steps.fix: Fold and serve immediately; make them one at a time.

steps.do: Wipe the pan, re-oil lightly and repeat with the remaining batter and eggs.
steps.look: Each crêpe takes about 2 minutes once you have the rhythm.
steps.mistake: Letting the pan overheat between crêpes.
steps.fix: Take it off the heat for 20 seconds between crêpes if it starts to smoke.

science: Mung bean flour gives the crêpe a slightly springy, tender texture and an earthy flavour; it has no gluten, so it is blended with wheat flour for stretch and strength. A thin batter spread on medium heat sets quickly as the starch gelatinises and the water evaporates, leaving a sheet flexible enough to fold. The egg sets in the same short time because it is spread thin. The fried cracker stays crisp because frying drives out nearly all its water; the moment it meets moist sauce and steam it starts to soften, which is why speed matters. Oil at 350°F (175°C) seals and puffs the wrapper quickly, so it absorbs less fat.
plating: Jian bing is eaten from a paper bag on the move. At home, cut each parcel in half on the diagonal to show the layers and serve two halves standing on a plate, with extra chilli oil on the side.

pairing.drink: Warm, lightly sweetened soy milk, the classic Beijing breakfast drink, or a pot of jasmine tea.

variations: Use a strip of crisp fried dough (youtiao) in place of the crackers.
Add a lettuce leaf and a slice of ham for a heartier version.
Make it vegetarian with fried tofu skin instead of the crackers.
safety: Hot oil: fill the pan no more than a third full, keep the thermometer in, never leave it unattended, and keep a lid nearby to smother a fire. Never use water on burning oil.

title: Tamales Rojos
summary: Corn husks spread with masa beaten light with lard and filled with pork in a red chile sauce, then steamed until the masa sets. It is here because it teaches masa by feel, the float test that tells you the fat is beaten in enough, a long braise and steaming in leaves.
skills: beating lard into masa until it floats
equipment: Large heavy pot with a lid, for braising
Stand mixer with a paddle, or a large bowl and strong arms
Large tamale steamer or a stockpot with a steamer basket and a lid
Two coins, for the bottom of the steamer
Large bowl for soaking the husks
Spoon or offset spatula for spreading

ingredients.note: 2 for the pork, 3 for the sauce

ingredients.item: Lard or vegetable shortening, for frying the sauce

ingredients.us: 1 1/2 tsp, plus more for the pork

mise: Soak the husks in a large bowl of hot water, weighted with a plate, for at least 1 hour until pliable.
Toast the dried chillies in a dry pan for 15 to 20 seconds a side until fragrant, then soak in hot water 20 minutes.
Put two coins in the bottom of the steamer pot with about 2 inches (5 cm) of water below the basket.
Bring the lard to room temperature so it beats easily.

timeline.do: Braise the pork; soak husks and chillies.
Make the red sauce and shred the pork into it.
Beat the masa to the float test.
Spread, fill and fold.
Steam.
Rest 15 minutes and serve.

steps.do: Put the pork in the heavy pot with the onion, 2 garlic cloves, bay leaf and 1 tsp (6 g) salt and cover with 6 cups (1.4 litres) water. Bring to the boil, skim, then simmer gently covered for 1 1/2 to 2 hours until it shreds easily.
steps.look: The meat breaks apart with no effort when pressed with a fork; the broth is golden and savoury.
steps.mistake: Boiling hard, which makes the meat dry and stringy.
steps.fix: Keep it at a lazy simmer. If short of time, use the pressure cooker for 35 minutes.

steps.do: Lift out the pork and keep the broth. Blend the drained chillies with the 3 remaining garlic cloves, cumin, oregano and 1 1/2 cups (360 ml) of broth until very smooth, then push through a sieve.
steps.look: A smooth, brick-red sauce that smells fruity and earthy, with no bits of skin.
steps.mistake: Skipping the sieve, so tough chilli skins end up in the tamales.
steps.fix: Push it through with the back of a ladle; it takes two minutes.

steps.do: Heat the 1 tbsp (13 g) lard in a saucepan over medium-high heat, pour in the sauce (it will spit) and fry, stirring, for 5 minutes. Simmer 10 minutes more, season with salt, then shred the pork into it.
steps.look: The sauce darkens and thickens enough to coat the pork; it tastes deep and slightly sweet.
steps.mistake: A thin sauce, which runs out of the tamales.
steps.fix: Simmer until thick enough to cling; the filling should be moist but not wet.

steps.do: Beat the masa. In the mixer, beat the lard on medium-high for 3 minutes until white and fluffy. In another bowl, mix masa harina, baking powder and salt with 2 cups (480 ml) warm broth into a soft dough. Add the dough to the lard in four lots, beating well after each, then beat 5 minutes more, adding broth a little at a time.
steps.look: A soft, light paste, like thick hummus, that spreads easily.
steps.mistake: Under-beating, so the tamales are heavy and dense.
steps.fix: Keep beating; the air you add now is what makes them light.

steps.do: Do the float test: drop 1/2 tsp (about 3 g) of masa into a glass of cold water.
steps.look: It floats.
steps.mistake: Moving on when it sinks, which gives tamales like bricks.
steps.fix: Beat 2 to 3 minutes more and test again; add a spoonful of lard if it still sinks.

steps.do: Pat a husk dry and lay it smooth side up, the wide end towards you. Spread about 3 tbsp (about 50 g) of masa in a thin layer over the wide half, leaving 1 inch (2.5 cm) bare along one long side and the narrow end.
steps.look: An even rectangle of masa about 1/4 inch (6 mm) thick.
steps.mistake: Spreading too thick, so the masa never cooks through in the centre.
steps.fix: Thin and even; it puffs as it steams.

steps.do: Spoon 1 1/2 tbsp (about 25 g) of filling down the centre. Fold the masa-covered side over the filling, then roll so the bare edge wraps round. Fold the narrow tail up. Tie with a strip of husk if it unfolds.
steps.look: A neat parcel with the filling sealed inside the masa.
steps.mistake: Overfilling, so the filling breaks through.
steps.fix: Use less filling; the masa is the point.

steps.do: Stand the tamales upright, open end up, packed snugly in the steamer basket. Cover with a layer of spare husks and a damp tea towel, then the lid. Steam over medium heat for 75 to 90 minutes.
steps.look: The coins rattle steadily, which tells you there is still water in the pot.
steps.mistake: Letting the pot boil dry, which burns the pot and leaves the tamales raw.
steps.fix: When the rattling stops, top up with boiling water from the kettle at once.

steps.do: Test one: take it out, rest it 2 minutes, then unwrap.
steps.look: The masa pulls cleanly away from the husk and is firm and fluffy throughout.
steps.mistake: Unwrapping too soon, while the masa sticks and is pasty.
steps.fix: Steam 15 minutes more and test again.

steps.do: Turn off the heat and leave the tamales in the steamer, covered, for 15 minutes before serving.
steps.look: They firm up as they rest and hold their shape when unwrapped.
steps.mistake: Serving straight from the steam, when they are still soft and fragile.
steps.fix: Resting is part of the cooking; do not skip it.

science: Masa is corn treated with lime, a process called nixtamalisation, which loosens the hull and changes the corn's proteins so the dough holds together. Beating lard into it traps tiny air bubbles, and the float test shows when there is enough air to make the masa lighter than water. In the steamer, the air bubbles and the baking powder's carbon dioxide expand while the corn starch gelatinises around them, setting a light, tender crumb. Steam transfers heat efficiently and evenly without drying the masa, and the husk holds the shape and adds a faint flavour. Frying the chilli sauce in hot fat cooks the raw chilli edge away and deepens its colour.
plating: Serve in their husks on a platter, a few opened to show the red filling, with Mexican crema, a salsa verde and a pickled onion salad on the side. Guests unwrap their own; the husk is never eaten.

pairing.drink: A café de olla, Mexican coffee spiced with cinnamon and piloncillo, or a Mexican hot chocolate.

variations: Tamales verdes: chicken in a tomatillo and green chilli sauce.
Rajas con queso: strips of roasted poblano and a little cheese, a vegetarian filling.
Steam in banana leaves for Oaxacan-style tamales with a softer, more delicate masa.
safety: Steam burns badly: open the lid away from you and lift tamales out with tongs.
Cool leftover tamales quickly and refrigerate within 2 hours; reheat by steaming until the centre is piping hot, 165°F (74°C).

title: Doubles
summary: Trinidad's street breakfast: two soft, turmeric-yellow fried breads called bara, with curried chickpeas spooned between them and finished with tamarind sauce, cucumber chutney and pepper sauce. It is here because it builds on frying yeast dough, stretched very thin with oiled hands, and on a slow curried chickpea pot thickened by its own crushed peas.
skills: a turmeric yeast dough stretched thin and fried
equipment: Large mixing bowl and cling film
Medium heavy saucepan with a lid
Small saucepan for the tamarind sauce
Deep heavy pan or wok for frying
Wire rack over a tray lined with kitchen paper
A plate brushed with oil, for stretching the dough

ingredients.note: plus a little for your hands
or 1 cup (200 g) dried, soaked and cooked very soft

ingredients.item: Chadon beni (culantro) or coriander leaves, chopped

ingredients.note: with lime juice and garlic for the chutney

mise: Soak the tamarind in 1 cup (240 ml) hot water for 20 minutes.
Chop the onion, garlic and chadon beni.
Grate and squeeze the cucumber, then mix with a squeeze of lime, a little minced garlic, chopped chadon beni and salt.
Oil a large plate and your work surface lightly.

timeline.do: Make the dough and leave it to rise.
Curry the chickpeas.
Make the tamarind sauce and the cucumber chutney.
Divide the dough, rest, heat the oil.
Stretch and fry the bara.
Assemble and eat at once.

steps.do: Mix the flour, yeast, turmeric, cumin, sugar and salt. Add the warm water and mix to a very soft, slightly sticky dough. Knead 3 minutes in the bowl, cover and leave to rise 1 to 1 1/2 hours.
steps.look: A soft, slack, yellow dough that doubles in size and is full of bubbles.
steps.mistake: Adding flour to make it easy to handle, which gives tough bara.
steps.fix: Keep it soft; you will handle it with oiled hands, not flour.

steps.do: Heat 2 tbsp (30 ml) oil in the saucepan over medium heat. Fry the onion and garlic 3 minutes. Stir the curry powder with 3 tbsp (45 ml) water into a paste, add it and fry 2 minutes until it darkens and the oil separates.
steps.look: A thick, fragrant paste, the raw spice smell turning toasted and deep.
steps.mistake: Adding dry curry powder straight into hot oil, which burns it.
steps.fix: The water paste protects the spices while they cook.

steps.do: Add the chickpeas and stir to coat, then add 1 1/2 cups (360 ml) water and 1 tsp (6 g) salt. Cover and simmer 30 to 40 minutes, stirring now and then, crushing some chickpeas against the side of the pan.
steps.look: Very soft chickpeas in a thick, yellow, spoonable sauce.
steps.mistake: A watery channa that runs off the bara.
steps.fix: Simmer uncovered for the last 10 minutes and crush more chickpeas to thicken. Stir in chadon beni at the end.

steps.do: Make the tamarind sauce: push the soaked tamarind through a sieve, then simmer the pulp with the brown sugar, a minced garlic clove, a pinch of salt and a pinch of chilli for 10 minutes until syrupy.
steps.look: A dark, glossy sauce that coats a spoon, sweet and sharply sour.
steps.mistake: Too thick, so it does not drizzle.
steps.fix: Loosen with a spoonful of water.

steps.do: Divide the risen dough into 12 pieces with oiled hands and roll into balls. Set on the oiled plate, cover and rest 15 minutes.
steps.look: Soft round balls that relax and spread a little.
steps.mistake: Letting them stick together.
steps.fix: Space them well apart on the oiled plate.

steps.do: Heat the oil in the deep pan to 350°F (175°C).
steps.look: The thermometer holds steady at 350°F (175°C).
steps.mistake: Frying in oil that is too cool, so the bara soak up fat.
steps.fix: Wait for the thermometer; heat between batches.

steps.do: Oil your fingers and press a ball flat on the oiled plate, then stretch it with your fingers into a very thin round about 4 1/2 inches (11 cm) across. It should be almost see-through in places.
steps.look: A thin, soft disc that holds together when lifted.
steps.mistake: Leaving them thick, which makes them bready and heavy.
steps.fix: Press out from the centre; small holes are fine.

steps.do: Lay the bara gently into the oil, away from you. It puffs within seconds. Fry 10 to 15 seconds, turn with the spider, fry 10 seconds more and lift onto the rack.
steps.look: The bara puffs up, turns pale golden and stays soft and pliable, not crisp.
steps.mistake: Frying too long, so it turns crisp and brown.
steps.fix: Seconds, not minutes; it should bend without cracking.

steps.do: Lay two bara overlapping on a square of paper or a plate, spoon channa over, add tamarind sauce, cucumber chutney and pepper sauce to taste, and fold the bottom bara up. Eat at once.
steps.look: Soft yellow bread, spilling chickpeas, glossy sauces.
steps.mistake: Building them ahead, so the bara soak and fall apart.
steps.fix: Assemble to order, as the vendors do.

science: The bara is a very wet yeast dough. The high water content means the dough is soft and extensible, and when it hits hot oil the water turns to steam and the yeast's carbon dioxide expands, puffing it within seconds. Because it fries so briefly, only the very surface dries and colours, so the bread stays soft rather than crisp. Turmeric is fat soluble, which is why the colour intensifies in the oil. In the channa, crushing some chickpeas releases their starch, which thickens the sauce without flour. Cooking curry powder in oil first matters because many of the flavour compounds in the spices dissolve in fat, not water, and toasting them removes the raw, dusty taste.
plating: Doubles are wrapped in greaseproof paper and eaten from the hand. At home, serve them on small squares of paper on a board, with the sauces in small bowls so everyone chooses 'slight pepper' or 'heavy pepper'.

pairing.drink: A cold mauby or sorrel, or a glass of fresh coconut water to cool the pepper.

variations: Make the bara with a pinch of bicarbonate as well as yeast for an even softer puff.
Add a spoonful of kuchela, a spicy grated green mango pickle.
Serve the channa alone with roti as a curry.
safety: Hot oil: fill the pan no more than a third full, lay the bara in away from you, and keep a lid nearby. Never put water on burning oil.
Wash your hands after handling Scotch bonnet sauce and keep them away from your eyes.

title: Pão de Queijo
summary: Brazilian cheese bread: a dough of sour tapioca starch scalded with hot milk and oil, then beaten with eggs and cheese and baked into small rolls that are crisp outside and hollow, chewy and stretchy inside. It is here because it is made exactly like choux, a cooked paste beaten with egg, and rehearses that method before the pastry kitchen asks for it.
skills: scalding tapioca starch with milk and oil
equipment: Stand mixer with a paddle, or a large bowl and a wooden spoon
Two baking trays lined with baking paper
Small bowl of oil for your hands

ingredients.note: or half sour and half sweet tapioca starch

ingredients.item: Low-moisture mozzarella or Minas cheese, grated

mise: Heat the oven to 400°F (200°C) with racks in the upper and lower thirds.
Line the trays.
Grate both cheeses.
Weigh the starch into the mixer bowl.
Beat the eggs in a jug.

timeline.do: Heat the oven, weigh and grate.
Scald the starch.
Beat in eggs and cheese.
Roll the balls.
Bake.
Serve warm.

steps.do: Bring the milk, water, oil and salt to a full boil in the saucepan over medium heat.
steps.look: The liquid rises and froths up the side of the pan.
steps.mistake: Taking it off just warm, so the starch is not scalded and the dough stays runny.
steps.fix: Wait for a rolling boil; the heat is what cooks the starch.

steps.do: Pour the boiling liquid over the starch all at once and mix with the paddle on low, or a wooden spoon, until no dry starch remains.
steps.look: A lumpy, sticky, translucent mass that looks wrong, like glue and gravel.
steps.mistake: Thinking it has failed and adding more liquid.
steps.fix: This is right; keep going.

steps.do: Mix on medium for 3 to 5 minutes until the dough is smoother and has cooled to warm, about 120°F (49°C).
steps.look: A smoother, stretchy, sticky dough, warm but not hot to touch.
steps.mistake: Adding the eggs while the dough is too hot, so they cook in streaks.
steps.fix: Wait a few more minutes, mixing to release heat.

steps.do: Add the beaten eggs a little at a time, mixing well after each addition until absorbed.
steps.look: The dough first breaks into slippery pieces, then comes back together, glossy and sticky.
steps.mistake: Adding all the egg at once, which leaves a soupy mess.
steps.fix: Add slowly; if it stays very loose, chill it 20 minutes before shaping.

steps.do: Mix in both cheeses until evenly spread.
steps.look: A soft, sticky, cheesy dough that holds a shape when scooped.
steps.mistake: Overworking after the cheese, which can make it greasy.
steps.fix: Mix just until combined.

steps.do: Oil your hands and roll the dough into balls about 1 1/4 inches (3 cm) across, about 30 g each. Space them 2 inches (5 cm) apart on the trays.
steps.look: Smooth, shiny balls.
steps.mistake: Dry hands, so the dough sticks everywhere.
steps.fix: Re-oil your hands every few balls.

steps.do: Bake 20 to 25 minutes, swapping the trays halfway, until puffed and golden with a few cracks.
steps.look: Balls double in size, puff into rounds with crackled, golden tops, and sound hollow when tapped.
steps.mistake: Taking them out pale, so they collapse as they cool.
steps.fix: Bake until truly golden; pale ones sink.

steps.do: Cool 5 minutes on the tray and serve warm.
steps.look: A crisp shell giving way to a stretchy, chewy, hollow inside that pulls in strings.
steps.mistake: Serving cold, when they are leathery.
steps.fix: Reheat in a hot oven for 4 minutes.

science: Tapioca starch is extracted from cassava and contains no gluten. Pouring boiling liquid over it gelatinises part of the starch, swelling the granules into a sticky paste, the same principle as cooking a choux paste on the hob. That paste can hold eggs, whose water and proteins loosen it into a dough that traps steam. In the oven the water turns to steam and the dough balloons, while the starch and egg proteins set into a stretchy, elastic shell; the inside is left partly hollow. Tapioca's high proportion of amylopectin is what gives the distinctive chew. Sour tapioca starch has been fermented, which changes its starch so it expands more in the oven and adds a gentle tang.
plating: Pile them warm in a cloth-lined basket so the steam stays in. Serve with salted butter and a small bowl of guava paste or a strong coffee.

pairing.drink: A strong café com leite or a cortado, whose bitterness cuts the salty cheese.

variations: Freeze the shaped raw balls on a tray, then bag them; bake straight from frozen for 25 to 30 minutes.
Add chopped chives or a pinch of chilli flakes with the cheese.
Use a mild cheddar in place of mozzarella for a stronger flavour.
safety: Boiling milk and oil spits and burns; pour it slowly and keep your face away.

title: Khachapuri Adjaruli
summary: The Georgian cheese boat: a soft yeast dough shaped into an open boat, filled with salty melting cheese, baked until bronzed and finished with an egg yolk and butter stirred in at the table. It is here because it teaches shaping a dough that must hold a molten centre without splitting, and how residual heat finishes an egg.
skills: adding egg and butter at the end
equipment: Baking stone or a heavy upturned baking tray

ingredients.item: Feta or sulguni and imeruli, crumbled

mise: Warm the milk and water together to about 100°F (38°C).
Grate and crumble the cheeses, mix them, and stir in 2 tbsp (30 ml) water or milk to help them melt smoothly.
Put the stone or upturned tray on the middle shelf and heat the oven to its maximum, ideally 475°F (245°C), for at least 30 minutes.
Separate the two yolks and keep each in its half shell or a small cup.

timeline.do: Mix and knead the dough.
First rise.
Heat the oven and stone.
Shape the boats and fill.
Bake.
Add yolk and butter, return briefly, serve.

steps.do: Mix the flour, yeast, sugar and salt, add the warm milk and water and the oil, and knead 8 minutes until smooth.
steps.look: A soft, smooth, slightly tacky dough that springs back slowly when poked.
steps.mistake: Adding lots of flour, which makes it tough.
steps.fix: Knead on a lightly oiled surface instead of a floured one.

steps.do: Cover and rise in a warm place for 1 hour until doubled.
steps.look: A puffy dough that holds a finger dent.
steps.mistake: Rushing a cold dough.
steps.fix: Give it longer in a warmer spot.

steps.do: Divide into 2 pieces and roll each into an oval about 12 by 8 inches (30 by 20 cm) and 1/4 inch (6 mm) thick on baking paper.
steps.look: Two even ovals.
steps.mistake: Rolling too thin, so the base tears under the cheese.
steps.fix: Keep it a little thicker in the middle.

steps.do: Roll each long side of the oval in towards the centre, about 1 1/2 inches (4 cm), to form two thick rims, leaving an open middle. Pinch and twist the two ends together firmly to make pointed boat ends.
steps.look: A canoe shape with thick, rolled sides and firmly sealed, twisted points.
steps.mistake: Loosely sealed ends, which open in the oven and let the cheese escape.
steps.fix: Pinch hard and give each end two full twists.

steps.do: Gently stretch the boat a little wider in the centre and fill the hollow with the cheese mixture, mounding it slightly. Brush the rims with beaten egg.
steps.look: A full boat with a golden-washed rim.
steps.mistake: Overfilling right to the edge of the rims, so it spills.
steps.fix: Keep the cheese inside the walls; it puffs as it melts.

steps.do: Slide the boats on their paper onto the hot stone and bake 12 to 15 minutes.
steps.look: The crust turns deep bronze and the cheese bubbles and browns in spots.
steps.mistake: Pale crust from an oven not hot enough.
steps.fix: Bake longer, watching carefully, or move to a higher shelf for the last 2 minutes.

steps.fix: One minute is often enough; the stirring finishes it.

Large heavy frying pan or flat griddle
Small frying pan for the tempering

ingredients.item: Yellow split lentils (toor dal) or red lentils

Slice the shallots and garlic; pick the curry leaves.
Oil the shallow container well.
Clear and oil a large smooth worktop for stretching.

Cook the lentils.
Stretch and coil the dough; rest the coils.
Temper the dhal.
Flatten and griddle the roti.
Clap and serve with the dhal.

steps.mistake: Making it stiff, so it tears instead of stretching.
steps.fix: Knead in more water a little at a time; softer is better.

steps.look: Next day the balls are soft and relaxed, slumping slightly, and spread easily under the finger.
steps.mistake: Resting too short, so the dough springs back and tears.
steps.fix: Give it longer. Dough that fights back needs more rest, not more force.

steps.look: Lentils collapsed into a smooth, yellow, pourable purée.
steps.mistake: Undercooked lentils, still firm and grainy.
steps.fix: Simmer longer, adding hot water if it thickens too much.

steps.do: Take one ball, flatten it on the oiled worktop with your oiled palm, then push and stretch it outwards from the centre with your fingertips. Lift the edge and gently pull, working round, until it is a very thin sheet about 18 inches (45 cm) across.
steps.look: A translucent sheet you can see the worktop through, with a few small holes at the edges.
steps.mistake: Pulling too hard in one place, which tears a large hole.
steps.fix: Small holes do not matter. Work evenly round the edge, letting the oiled surface hold the dough in place.

steps.do: Fold the sheet: bring the two opposite edges into the middle, then fold the other two sides in, making a square. Or gather the sheet into a long rope, pleating it like a curtain, and coil the rope into a snail, tucking the end under.
steps.look: A small, layered square or a coiled snail, thick with folds.
steps.mistake: Folding without oil, so the layers stick together.
steps.fix: Brush a little more ghee over the sheet before folding.

steps.do: Rest the folded roti for 10 minutes, then press each gently into a round about 6 inches (15 cm) across.
steps.look: A flattened round with visible spiral or folded layers.
steps.mistake: Pressing too hard, which squashes the layers together.
steps.fix: Press lightly with your fingertips.

steps.do: Make the tempering: heat the oil in the small pan over medium heat, add mustard and cumin seeds and the chillies; when the seeds pop add curry leaves, shallots and garlic and fry until golden. Pour into the dhal.
steps.look: A loud sizzle and a burst of aroma as it hits the dhal.
steps.mistake: Burning the garlic and shallots.
steps.fix: Take the pan off the heat as soon as they are golden.

steps.do: Heat the frying pan over medium heat with 1 tsp (5 ml) ghee. Cook each roti 2 to 3 minutes a side, pressing with the fish slice, until golden with dark spots and crisp at the edges.
steps.look: Blistered, golden layers that puff slightly, smelling of toasted ghee.
steps.mistake: Too high a heat, which burns the outside before the inside layers cook.
steps.fix: Lower the heat; it should sizzle steadily, not smoke.

steps.do: Lift the hot roti onto the worktop and clap it between your palms from the sides, or scrunch it inwards with both hands, to break open the layers.
steps.look: The roti fluffs up and the layers separate into flaky leaves.
steps.mistake: Skipping this, so the layers stay flattened together.
steps.fix: Clap quickly while it is hot; use a cloth if it is too hot to handle.

steps.do: Serve straight away with bowls of dhal for dipping.
steps.look: Flaky, chewy bread and a fragrant yellow curry.
steps.mistake: Stacking the hot roti, which steams them soft.
steps.fix: Keep them on a rack or in a cloth-lined basket, uncovered.

Coating the dough in oil stops a dry skin forming and lets the dough slide over the worktop as it stretches. When the thin sheet is folded with fat between the layers, the fat keeps the layers apart. On the griddle, water in each layer turns to steam and pushes them apart, while the fat fries them crisp. Clapping breaks the layers open while they are still soft and hot.

pairing.drink: Teh tarik, strong tea pulled with condensed milk until frothy, the classic mamak stall partner.

variations: Roti telur: crack an egg onto the stretched sheet before folding.
Roti bawang: scatter sliced red onion over the sheet before folding.
Serve with a chicken or fish curry in place of the dhal.
safety: Clapping a roti straight from the pan can burn your palms; let it cool for a few seconds or use a clean cloth.
Do not leave the frying pan unattended with ghee in it.

title: Feteer Meshaltet

Round baking tin or ovenproof frying pan, 9 to 10 inch (23 to 25 cm)

ingredients.note: or clarify 1 cup (225 g) of unsalted butter

ingredients.item: Honey, molasses with tahini, or thick cream
Salty white cheese such as feta

Grease the worktop generously with clarified butter.
Heat the oven to 425°F (220°C) with a rack in the lower third.
Grease the tin with clarified butter.

Divide, coat in samna, rest 45 minutes.
Stretch and fold each piece.
Stack and press into the tin.
Bake.

steps.look: A soft, smooth, supple dough that stretches easily.
steps.mistake: Kneading for a long time, which makes the gluten strong and the dough fights back when stretched.
steps.fix: Five minutes is enough; then rest it.

steps.do: Divide into 6 pieces, roll each into a ball and roll it through the warm samna until slick. Cover with the cloth and rest 45 minutes.
steps.look: Balls that have relaxed so a poke leaves a dent that does not spring back.
steps.mistake: Not resting long enough, so the dough tears when stretched.
steps.fix: If it springs back, rest 20 minutes more in a warm place.

steps.do: On the greased worktop, press one ball flat with your palm and push it outwards from the centre with your fingertips, then lift and stretch the edges, until it is a sheet thin enough to read newsprint through, about 16 inches (40 cm) across.
steps.look: A thin, translucent sheet with a few small holes at the edges.
steps.mistake: Using flour on the worktop, which glues the layers together.
steps.fix: Use only fat on the surface and your hands; holes at the edges do not matter.

steps.do: Brush the sheet with samna. Fold the left third over the middle, then the right third over that. Brush again, then fold the top third down and the bottom third up to make a small square parcel about 4 inches (10 cm) across.
steps.look: A neat, layered square, buttery on every surface.
steps.mistake: Folding a dry sheet, which makes layers stick.
steps.fix: Brush every surface before folding.

steps.do: Repeat with the other balls. Then stretch the next sheet, place a folded parcel in its centre, and fold the sheet round it. Do the same with two more, so you end with two large parcels, each with layers inside layers.
steps.look: Two thick, buttery parcels with many layers.
steps.mistake: Working fast and tearing big holes in the outer sheet.
steps.fix: Patch tears by folding the edge over; the outside sheet holds everything in.

steps.do: Lay one parcel in the tin and press and stretch it gently with your fingertips to fill the base. Brush with samna, then lay the second parcel on top and press it out to cover. Brush the top generously.
steps.look: A round, even disc filling the tin, glossy with fat.
steps.mistake: Pressing so hard that the layers merge.
steps.fix: Use flat fingertips and gentle pressure.

steps.do: Bake 25 to 30 minutes until puffed, blistered and a deep mahogany gold, the base crisp.
steps.look: The top layers lift and separate, crackling, and the edges turn deep golden.
steps.mistake: Pale, soft feteer from too short a bake.
steps.fix: Bake longer; colour is flavour and crispness.

steps.do: Brush with a little more samna as it comes out, cool 5 minutes, then cut into wedges and serve with honey or cheese.

pairing.drink: Strong mint tea or Egyptian black tea with sugar, which cuts the butter.

variations: Savoury: scatter crumbled cheese and diced pastrami or sausage between the parcels.
Sweet: scatter sugar and nuts between the layers and pour hot syrup over after baking.
Bake as individual small parcels for a quicker version.
safety: Hot clarified butter burns: melt it gently and keep it warm, not sizzling, for brushing.
The tin is very hot coming out of the oven; use oven gloves.

title: Kouglof Alsacien

a slow proof and an even bake

Mix and knead the dough, add the butter.
First rise, then fold in raisins and fill the mould.
Second proof in the mould.
Bake.
Turn out, cool, dust.

steps.do: Put the flour, sugar, salt, yeast, milk and eggs in the mixer bowl. Mix on low for 3 minutes, then medium for 8 to 10 minutes.
steps.look: The dough slaps against the bowl and pulls away cleanly from the sides, and a small piece stretches into a thin, translucent window.
steps.mistake: Adding butter before the gluten has developed, which gives a heavy, crumbly cake.
steps.fix: Keep kneading until the window test passes; it can take 12 minutes.

steps.do: With the mixer on medium, add the soft butter in four additions, letting each disappear before the next.
steps.look: The dough first looks greasy and breaks up, then comes back together glossy, soft and elastic.
steps.mistake: Letting the dough get warm, which melts the butter into an oily mess.
steps.fix: Check with the thermometer; above 75°F (24°C), stop and chill the bowl for 15 minutes.

steps.do: Drain the raisins and mix them in on low for 30 seconds, just until spread through.
steps.look: Raisins evenly distributed, not crushed.
steps.mistake: Mixing too long, which tears the gluten and crushes fruit.
steps.fix: Finish folding them in by hand if needed.

steps.do: Cover and rise at room temperature for 1 1/2 hours, until nearly doubled.
steps.look: A soft, puffy dough, wobbly when the bowl is shaken.
steps.mistake: A cold kitchen where it barely moves.
steps.fix: Leave longer in a warmer spot, about 75°F (24°C).

steps.do: Knock back gently, shape into a ball, push your thumbs through the centre to make a ring and drop it into the mould, pressing evenly. It should fill about a third of the mould.
steps.look: An even ring of dough sitting over the almonds.
steps.mistake: Uneven depth, so it rises lopsided.
steps.fix: Press it level with your fingers.

steps.do: Cover and proof 1 1/2 to 2 hours, until the dough rises to about 1/2 inch (1 cm) below the rim and wobbles when nudged. Heat the oven to 350°F (180°C) with a rack in the lower third.
steps.look: A domed, airy dough that springs back slowly when lightly pressed, leaving a small dent.
steps.mistake: Overproofing, so it collapses in the oven.
steps.fix: If it springs back instantly it needs longer; if the dent stays and the dough sighs, bake immediately.

steps.do: Bake 35 to 40 minutes, covering loosely with foil after 20 minutes if it is browning fast, until deep golden and the centre reads 195 to 200°F (90 to 93°C).
steps.look: A deep chestnut crust and a hollow sound when tapped.
steps.mistake: Pulling it out pale and under-baked, which leaves a gummy middle.
steps.fix: Use the thermometer; colour can mislead in a deep mould.

steps.do: Turn out onto the rack at once and cool completely. Dust with icing sugar just before serving.
steps.look: A tall, fluted cake with almonds crowning each ridge.
steps.mistake: Leaving it in the mould, where steam softens the crust and it sticks.

pairing.brennans: Brandy Milk Punch: Brennan's creamy brunch cocktail with brandy and nutmeg is the kind of drink that matches a buttery yeasted breakfast cake.

steps.mistake: A dough at 79°F (26°C) or more, which is greasy and slack because the butter is melting out.
steps.fix: Put the whole bowl in the fridge for 15 minutes, then mix briefly again.

title: Medialunas

Two baking trays lined with baking paper

ingredients.item: Unsalted butter, cold, for the block

mise: Make the butter block: put the cold butter between two sheets of baking paper and beat it with the rolling pin, then roll it into a square about 5 by 5 inches (13 by 13 cm). Chill.
Measure out the dough ingredients.
Make the syrup: boil the sugar, water and honey for 3 minutes, then cool.

Lock in the butter and make three letter folds, chilling 30 minutes between.
Roll, cut and shape.
Proof 1 1/2 to 2 hours.
Egg wash and bake.
Brush with syrup while hot.

steps.look: A smooth, firm dough, about the same firmness as the cold butter block.
steps.mistake: A soft, warm dough that butter will squeeze out of.
steps.fix: Chill it longer. Dough and butter must match in firmness.

steps.do: Take the butter out until it bends without cracking, about 55 to 60°F (13 to 16°C). Roll the dough into a square about 8 by 8 inches (20 by 20 cm). Set the butter on it turned like a diamond, fold the dough corners over to meet in the centre and pinch the seams closed.
steps.look: A neat envelope with no butter showing.
steps.mistake: Butter that is too cold and cracks into shards, or too soft and oozes.
steps.fix: If it cracks, leave it 5 minutes at room temperature; if soft, chill both 15 minutes.

steps.do: Roll the parcel into a rectangle about 6 by 16 inches (15 by 40 cm), rolling in short, even strokes from the centre outwards. Fold in thirds like a letter. That is fold one. Wrap and chill 30 minutes.
steps.look: An even rectangle with straight edges; the butter moves with the dough as one.
steps.mistake: Pressing so hard the butter breaks through.
steps.fix: If butter appears, dust the spot with flour and chill before carrying on.

steps.do: Repeat the rolling and letter fold twice more, chilling 30 minutes after each, turning the dough a quarter turn before each roll so the open edge faces you.
steps.look: Three folds give 27 layers; the dough feels smooth and the butter stays invisible.
steps.mistake: Rushing the chills, so the butter softens and merges with the dough.
steps.fix: Always chill; when in doubt, chill longer.

steps.do: Roll the dough to a rectangle 1/6 inch (4 mm) thick, about 10 by 16 inches (25 by 40 cm). Trim the edges. Cut tall, thin triangles with a base of about 3 inches (8 cm).
steps.look: Clean-cut triangles; on the cut edges you can see faint layers.
steps.mistake: Dragging a blunt knife, which squashes the layers together.
steps.fix: Use a sharp knife or pizza wheel with firm, single cuts.

steps.do: Make a small notch in the centre of each base, stretch the triangle gently longer, then roll it up from the base towards the tip, tightly. Bend the ends inwards into a crescent and set on the trays, tip underneath.
steps.look: Small, tightly rolled crescents with the tip tucked under.
steps.mistake: Rolling loosely, so they unroll in the oven.
steps.fix: Roll firmly and tuck the tip well under.

steps.look: Puffy crescents that jiggle when the tray is shaken, layers visible at the edges.
steps.mistake: Proofing somewhere warm, which melts the butter so it leaks onto the tray.
steps.fix: Keep below 80°F (27°C). If butter pools on the tray, the room is too warm.

steps.look: Puffed, flaky, glossy golden crescents.
steps.mistake: Pale, under-baked pastries that are doughy inside.
steps.fix: Bake until deep gold; the layers need colour to set crisp.

steps.do: As soon as they come out, brush generously with the syrup.
steps.look: A sticky, shiny glaze that sets as they cool.
steps.mistake: Waiting until they are cold, so the syrup sits on top and stays wet.
steps.fix: Brush within the first minute of leaving the oven.

science: Lamination makes layers of dough separated by sheets of butter. Each letter fold triples the layers, so three folds give 27. In the oven, the water in the butter and dough turns to steam and pushes the layers apart, while the melting fat fries them from the inside, giving flaky, airy pastry. Everything depends on butter and dough having the same firmness: if the butter is too hard it shatters into pieces, and if too soft it is absorbed into the dough and the layers vanish. Chilling between folds relaxes the gluten and firms the butter. The sugar and egg in this dough make it softer and quicker to brown than a croissant, and the hot syrup soaks in to give the sticky finish.

pairing.drink: A cortado or café con leche, the way Buenos Aires eats them.
pairing.brennans: New Orleans-Style Coffee with Chicory: the house coffee is the right partner for a sweet breakfast pastry and a good one to recommend with the Café Brûlot Coffee Cake.

variations: Medialunas de grasa: made with beef fat or lard, less sweet and flatter.
Fill with dulce de leche after baking.
Shape into straight croissants for a less curled pastry.
safety: Hot syrup sticks and burns; brush carefully and keep it away from children.

title: Croissants
summary: The French croissant: a lean yeast dough laminated with a cold block of butter in three folds, cut and rolled into crescents, proofed cool and baked until shattering outside and honeycombed within. equipment: Stand mixer with a dough hook
Rolling pin and a long ruler
Two baking trays lined with baking paper
A large plastic box or bag for proofing

ingredients.note: or half strong and half plain flour

ingredients.item: Unsalted butter, soft, for the dough
Unsalted butter, cold, for the block
ingredients.note: a high-fat European style butter, about 82% fat

ingredients.item: Egg beaten with milk, for the wash

Make the butter block (step 2) and chill it alongside the dough.
Clear and lightly flour a large worktop; have the ruler and a pastry brush for removing excess flour.
Make sure there is space in the fridge for a flat tray.

timeline.do: Mix the dough, shape a flat square, chill overnight; make the butter block.
Lock in the butter and make three letter folds, 30 minutes chilling between each.
Roll out, cut and shape.
Proof 2 to 2 1/2 hours at 75 to 78°F (24 to 26°C).
Heat the oven, egg wash, bake.
Cool 15 minutes on the rack and serve.

steps.look: A smooth, firm dough, not fully kneaded; it should still tear slightly when stretched.
steps.mistake: Kneading to a full window, which makes the dough elastic and hard to roll thin later.
steps.fix: Keep the mixing short; the folds will build the strength.

steps.do: For the block, put the cold butter between two sheets of baking paper, beat it flat with the rolling pin, then roll it into an even square of 6 by 6 inches (15 by 15 cm). Fold the paper round it to keep the edges straight and chill.
steps.look: A flat, even, pale square, pliable but cold.
steps.mistake: An uneven block with thick and thin patches, which gives uneven layers.
steps.fix: Roll it inside a folded paper parcel of exactly the right size so it fills the corners.

steps.do: Take the butter out until it bends without snapping, about 55 to 60°F (13 to 16°C). Roll the cold dough into a square of 9 by 9 inches (23 by 23 cm). Lay the butter on it as a diamond, fold the four corners of dough over to meet in the middle and seal the seams by pinching.
steps.look: A sealed square parcel; dough and butter feel equally firm when pressed.
steps.mistake: Butter colder than the dough, which shatters when you roll.
steps.fix: Check both with a finger: they should give in the same way. Wait or chill as needed.

steps.do: Roll the parcel away from you into a rectangle 8 by 20 inches (20 by 50 cm), keeping the corners square. Brush off the flour and fold it in thirds like a letter. Wrap and chill 30 minutes. That is the first fold.
steps.look: A neat rectangle with smooth surfaces; no butter showing or breaking through.
steps.mistake: Rolling across and back with heavy pressure, which pushes butter out at the ends.
steps.fix: Roll in short strokes from the middle outwards. Square the corners with the side of the pin.

steps.do: Give the dough a quarter turn so the folded edge is on your left. Roll and fold twice more in exactly the same way, chilling 30 minutes after each fold.
steps.look: After three folds, a smooth, firm dough; at the edges you can just see thin pale stripes of butter.
steps.mistake: Skipping the chill when the dough feels fine, so the butter warms and smears.
steps.fix: Chill every time. If the dough springs back while rolling, rest it 10 minutes.

steps.do: Chill 1 hour, then roll the dough into a long strip 8 inches (20 cm) wide and 1/6 inch (4 mm) thick, about 24 inches (60 cm) long. Lift the dough and let it relax back for a minute so it does not shrink when cut.
steps.look: A long even strip; held up to the light the cut ends show many fine layers.
steps.mistake: Rolling too thick, so the croissants are bready.
steps.fix: Roll in two goes with a rest between; aim for 4 mm.

steps.do: Cut tall triangles with a base of 4 1/2 inches (11 cm) along one long edge. Make a small notch in the middle of each base. Stretch each triangle gently by its tip, then roll it up from the base with even pressure, finishing with the tip underneath.
steps.look: Eight croissants with six or seven visible steps and the point tucked beneath.
steps.mistake: Pressing down hard as you roll, which squashes the layers.
steps.fix: Roll with light fingertips, letting the dough roll itself.

steps.do: Set them on the trays well apart, brush lightly with egg wash and put them in a large closed plastic box or bag with a mug of hot water. Proof at 75 to 78°F (24 to 26°C) for 2 to 2 1/2 hours.

steps.mistake: Proofing above 80°F (27°C), so butter melts and leaks onto the tray, giving flat, greasy croissants.
steps.fix: If butter pools, the room is too hot; move them somewhere cooler.

steps.do: Heat the oven to 400°F (200°C). Brush again with egg wash, gently, avoiding the cut edges. Bake 16 to 20 minutes, swapping trays halfway, until deep golden brown.
steps.look: A crackling, glossy, deep brown crust; they feel very light.
steps.mistake: Under-baking because they look golden early, leaving a doughy middle.
steps.fix: Bake until really brown; a pale croissant is a soft croissant.

steps.do: Cool on a rack for 15 minutes, then pull one open.
steps.look: A shattering crust and an open honeycomb of thin, buttery layers.
steps.mistake: Cutting with a knife immediately, which crushes the crumb.
steps.fix: Tear it with your hands to see the structure; cut only once cool.

science: A croissant is a stack of very thin dough layers separated by equally thin sheets of butter. In a hot oven, the water in the dough and in the butter, which is about 16% water, turns to steam and inflates each layer, while the butter melts and fries the dough from within, setting a crisp, honeycombed structure. Everything depends on the butter staying a continuous sheet. Below about 55°F (13°C) it is brittle and shatters into flakes when rolled; above about 68°F (20°C) it softens and is absorbed into the dough. High-fat butter is more plastic and stretches further. Resting relaxes gluten so the dough can be rolled thin without shrinking, and a cool proof lets yeast inflate the layers without melting the butter.
plating: Serve warm on a board or in a basket, piled loosely so the crusts are not crushed. Offer salted butter and a good jam, though a perfect croissant needs neither.

pairing.drink: A café crème or a strong coffee, whose bitterness balances the butter; for a celebratory brunch, a Blanc de Blancs Champagne.
pairing.brennans: New Orleans-Style Coffee with Chicory: the house coffee is what a guest wants with a breakfast pastry, and its roasted bitterness cuts butter well.

variations: Pain au chocolat: cut rectangles, roll round two sticks of dark chocolate.
Almond croissants: split day-old croissants, fill with frangipane, top with flaked almonds and bake again.
Ham and cheese: roll a strip of ham and Gruyère inside each triangle.
safety: The oven and trays are very hot; use oven gloves and keep the oven door away from your face as steam escapes.

title: Caesar Salad
summary: Cos lettuce dressed with an emulsion of coddled egg, garlic, anchovy, lemon and olive oil, finished with Parmesan and crisp garlic croutons. skills: coddling eggs or using pasteurised eggs
an anchovy, garlic and oil emulsion
equipment: Mortar and pestle, or a chef's knife and board
Salad spinner and clean tea towels

ingredients.note: 1 for the dressing, 1 for the croutons
plus 3 tbsp (45 ml) for the croutons
crusts on, torn into 3/4 inch (2 cm) pieces

mise: Heat the oven to 375°F (190°C).
Separate the cos leaves, wash in cold water, spin dry and roll in a clean towel; chill 20 minutes so they are cold and crisp.
Tear the bread into rough pieces.
Grate half the Parmesan and shave the rest.
Squeeze the lemon.
Bring a small pan of water to the boil for coddling the egg.

timeline.do: Heat oven, wash and chill the leaves.
Bake the croutons.
Coddle the egg and make the dressing.
Dress the leaves.
Croutons and shaved Parmesan on top; serve on cold plates.

steps.do: Toss the bread with 3 tbsp (45 ml) olive oil, a pinch of salt and 1 clove of garlic finely grated. Bake on the tray 10 to 12 minutes, turning once, until golden and crisp.
steps.look: Golden, crunchy croutons, crisp right through, smelling of toasted garlic.
steps.mistake: Pale croutons that turn soggy in the dressing.
steps.fix: Bake longer; they should crunch loudly when cooled.

steps.do: Coddle the egg: lower it into boiling water for exactly 1 minute, then into cold water. Crack it and scoop the yolk and the slightly thickened white into the bowl.
steps.look: A warm yolk, the white just clouded and thicker than raw.
steps.mistake: Boiling longer, which sets the yolk so it will not emulsify.
steps.fix: One minute only. If it sets, use a pasteurised yolk instead.

steps.do: Mash the remaining garlic clove and the anchovies with a pinch of salt in the mortar, or chop and scrape them with the flat of your knife, to a smooth paste.
steps.look: A smooth, grey-pink paste with no pieces of garlic.
steps.mistake: Leaving chunks of raw garlic, which bite harshly.
steps.fix: Keep scraping with the side of the blade and a pinch of salt as grit.

steps.do: Whisk the paste with the egg, mustard, lemon juice and Worcestershire until smooth.
steps.look: A loose, frothy, pale mixture.
steps.mistake: Adding oil before the base is well mixed.
steps.fix: Whisk the base for 30 seconds first.

steps.do: Whisk in the olive oil a few drops at a time, then in a thin stream, whisking constantly.
steps.look: The dressing thickens and turns creamy and glossy, like thin mayonnaise.
steps.mistake: Pouring the oil fast, so it splits into oily streaks.
steps.fix: Stop pouring and whisk hard. If it stays split, whisk it slowly into a teaspoon of mustard in a clean bowl.

steps.do: Whisk in the grated Parmesan and season with black pepper. Taste: it should be bold, salty, garlicky and sharp.
steps.look: A thick, pourable, savoury dressing.
steps.mistake: Seasoning with salt before the cheese and anchovy, so it ends up too salty.
steps.fix: Add the cheese first, then taste before any salt.

steps.do: Put the cold leaves in the large bowl, pour the dressing down the side and toss with your hands, lifting from the bottom, until every leaf is coated.
steps.look: Each leaf lacquered with a thin even coat, none drowned, none bare.
steps.mistake: Dressing warm or wet leaves, which go limp and dilute the dressing.
steps.fix: Dry the leaves thoroughly first; toss gently but thoroughly.

steps.do: Pile onto cold plates, scatter croutons and shaved Parmesan over and finish with black pepper. Serve at once.
steps.look: Crisp, glossy leaves with croutons and curls of cheese on top.
steps.mistake: Adding croutons too early, so they soften.
steps.fix: Add them last, just before serving.

science: A dressing like this is an emulsion: tiny oil droplets dispersed in a small amount of watery lemon juice. Left alone, oil and water separate. Egg yolk contains lecithin and proteins that sit at the surface of each droplet and keep them apart, and mustard adds more emulsifiers and fine particles that help. Adding oil slowly at first lets the emulsifiers coat each new droplet; pour too fast and the droplets merge. Coddling the egg for a minute warms the yolk and thickens the white slightly, giving more body without cooking out its emulsifying power. Anchovy and Parmesan both carry glutamates, which give a deep savoury taste. Cold, dry leaves stay crisp because their cells are full of water and the dressing clings rather than sliding off.
plating: Cold, wide plates or a chilled platter. Arrange whole leaves stacked loosely, curved side up so they hold dressing, croutons scattered over and Parmesan shaved in long curls. A lemon wedge on the side and pepper cracked from a height.

pairing.drink: A crisp, unoaked white such as Albariño, or a dry Manzanilla sherry whose salty tang loves anchovy.
pairing.brennans: Creole Caesar: Brennan's own Caesar, the one to taste and describe against your classic version.

variations: Add grilled chicken or prawns for a main course salad.
Grill halved cos hearts quickly over high heat before dressing for a charred Caesar.
Replace the anchovy with a little white miso for a vegetarian version, using a vegetarian Worcestershire.
safety: A coddled egg is barely cooked. For pregnant guests, the very young, the elderly or anyone with a weakened immune system, use a pasteurised egg.
Keep the dressing in the fridge and use it within 24 hours.

title: Salade Lyonnaise

Salad spinner and clean tea towel

ingredients.item: Smoked bacon or poitrine, in one piece
ingredients.note: cut into lardons 1/2 inch (1 cm) thick

ingredients.us: 2 tbsp, plus 4 tsp for the water

ingredients.item: Fine salt and coarse black pepper

Cut the lardons and cube the bread.
Chop the shallot.
Fill the wide saucepan with water and the 4 tsp (20 ml) vinegar and heat to 180°F (82°C).
Crack each egg into its own cup.

timeline.do: Prepare leaves, lardons, bread.
Render the lardons, fry the croutons.
Poach the eggs, hold them in warm water.
Make the warm dressing.
Toss and serve with an egg on each plate.

steps.do: Put the lardons in the cold, dry frying pan and set over medium-low heat. Cook 8 to 10 minutes, stirring, until the fat runs and the edges crisp but the centres are still tender.
steps.look: Plenty of clear fat in the pan, lardons golden at the edges, smelling of smoke.
steps.mistake: Starting in a hot pan, which seals the outside and traps the fat inside.
steps.fix: Always start cold so the fat melts out slowly.

steps.fix: Keep turning; take them out as soon as they are golden.

steps.do: Poach the eggs one or two at a time: drain each in the sieve for a few seconds, then slide into the 180°F (82°C) water. Poach 3 minutes, lift out and slip into a bowl of warm water to hold.
steps.look: Neat, oval eggs with set whites and yolks that swing loose inside.
steps.mistake: Boiling water that shreds the whites.
steps.fix: Lower the heat to a quiver.

steps.do: Pour off all but about 3 tbsp (45 ml) fat from the pan. Off the heat, add the shallot and let it soften 30 seconds, then whisk in the mustard, the 2 tbsp (30 ml) vinegar and the oil.
steps.look: A cloudy, slightly thickened, warm dressing that smells sharp and smoky.
steps.mistake: Adding the vinegar to a very hot pan, so it spits violently.
steps.fix: Let the pan cool for a minute first, then whisk away from your face.

steps.do: Season the dressing with pepper and taste; it should be sharp enough to make you notice it.
steps.look: A balanced, bold vinaigrette.
steps.mistake: Salting before tasting; the bacon fat is already salty.
steps.fix: Taste first and add salt only if needed.

steps.do: Put the frisée in the bowl, pour over the warm dressing and toss with the lardons and croutons until the leaves slump slightly but still crackle.
steps.look: Leaves glossy and just wilting at the edges, still crisp at the ribs.
steps.mistake: Tossing too long, so the leaves collapse.
steps.fix: Toss and serve within a minute.

steps.do: Divide between plates, lift each egg from the warm water, blot on kitchen paper and set on top. Grind pepper over.
steps.look: A tangle of frisée, bacon and croutons crowned with a trembling egg.
steps.mistake: A wet egg that waters down the dressing.
steps.fix: Always blot the egg first.

science: Rendering lardons slowly from a cold pan melts their fat out before the meat firms, giving plenty of clear fat and crisp edges with tender centres. Mustard acts as the emulsifier, holding fat and vinegar together briefly so the dressing looks cloudy rather than separated. Frisée has thick, ribbed, bitter leaves with stiff cell walls, so warm dressing softens them without turning them to slime, which would happen to soft lettuce. pairing.brennans: Louis Jadot Beaujolais-Villages 2021 (375 ml): a half bottle of Beaujolais from the Brennan's list is exactly the wine Lyon drinks with this salad.

Use dandelion leaves when in season.
Replace the bacon with smoked duck breast.
safety: Vinegar in hot fat spits: take the pan off the heat and let it cool for a minute first.
Use pasteurised eggs for vulnerable guests if the yolk is to be runny.

title: Vitello Tonnato

skills: a tuna mayonnaise made by hand
equipment: Saucepan just large enough to hold the meat and liquid
Bowl and whisk, or a stick blender and tall beaker

ingredients.item: Veal topside or eye of round
ingredients.note: in one neat piece, tied with string

ingredients.item: Neutral oil and mild olive oil, mixed

mise: Tie the veal into an even cylinder with string at 1 inch (2.5 cm) intervals.
Chop the vegetables.
Bring the egg yolk to room temperature.
Drain the tuna, rinse the capers.

Chill the veal.
Make the mayonnaise and tonnato sauce.
Slice the veal thin.
Coat with sauce.
Garnish and serve cool.

steps.do: Put the veal in the saucepan with the wine, vegetables, aromatics and salt and add cold water to just cover. Bring slowly to 180°F (82°C), the surface barely trembling, over medium-low heat.
steps.look: Small bubbles rising occasionally, no rolling boil, a little grey foam to skim.
steps.mistake: Boiling, which tightens the lean meat and makes it dry and grey.
steps.fix: Keep it at a quiver with the lid half on; skim off foam.

steps.look: Pale pink-beige meat, firm but yielding when pressed.
steps.mistake: Cooking it to well done, which makes it dry.

steps.mistake: Taking it out to cool on a board, where it dries.
steps.fix: Cooling in the liquid keeps it juicy. Keep the liquid for the sauce.

steps.do: Make the mayonnaise: whisk the yolk with the lemon juice and a pinch of salt, then whisk in the oil a few drops at a time, then in a thin stream, until thick.
steps.look: A thick, glossy, pale mayonnaise that holds a peak.
steps.mistake: Adding oil too fast, which splits it.
steps.fix: Whisk a split sauce slowly into a fresh yolk or a teaspoon of warm water in a clean bowl.

steps.do: Blend the tuna, anchovies and capers to a smooth paste, then blend in the mayonnaise. Loosen with cold poaching liquid until it pours like thick cream. Season with lemon and pepper.
steps.look: A smooth, pale, velvety sauce that coats a spoon thickly and tastes savoury, sharp and of the sea.
steps.mistake: A sauce too thick to coat the slices thinly.
steps.fix: Add more poaching liquid a spoon at a time.

steps.do: Remove the string and slice the cold veal across the grain as thinly as you can, about 1/8 inch (3 mm), in long single strokes.
steps.look: Even, pale pink slices that hold together.
steps.mistake: Slicing warm meat or sawing, which tears it.
steps.fix: It must be cold; use the whole length of a sharp blade.

steps.do: Spread a thin layer of sauce on the platter, lay the slices overlapping on top, then spoon more sauce over to cover completely.
steps.look: A smooth white blanket with the outline of the slices just showing.
steps.mistake: Leaving meat exposed, which dries and darkens.
steps.fix: Cover every slice; the sauce protects it.

steps.do: Rest 10 minutes in the fridge, then garnish with capers and a few drops of olive oil. Serve cool, not fridge-cold.
steps.look: Capers dotted across a creamy surface.
steps.mistake: Serving straight from the fridge, when the flavours are muted.
steps.fix: Take it out 15 minutes before serving.

science: Lean veal has little fat or connective tissue to keep it moist, so its juiciness depends on not overcooking. Muscle proteins begin to contract and squeeze out water above about 140°F (60°C); poaching gently and stopping close to that point keeps the meat tender. Cooling in the liquid lets the temperature equalise and the meat reabsorb some liquid. Mayonnaise is an emulsion of oil droplets in a little water, held stable by the lecithin and proteins in egg yolk. Blending in tuna and anchovy adds savoury flavour and fine particles that thicken it further, and poaching liquid both thins it to a coating consistency and ties the sauce to the meat.
plating: A large flat platter, slices overlapping in a single rose or straight rows, the sauce smoothed to the edges with a palette knife, capers scattered or set in a neat line, a few caper berries and lemon wedges at one end.

pairing.drink: A Barbera d'Asti or a light Nebbiolo from Piedmont, the dish's home: bright acidity and soft tannin suit veal and the rich sauce.
pairing.brennans: La Miraja ‘Le Masche’ Barbera d’Asti 2023: a Piedmont Barbera on the Brennan's list, from the same region as the dish.

variations: Use pork loin poached the same way.
Make it with leftover roast veal or turkey breast, sliced thin.
Make the sauce the older way, without mayonnaise, by blending tuna with hard-boiled yolks and poaching liquid.
safety: Whole cuts of veal are safe at 145°F (63°C) held for 3 minutes; cooling the meat in its liquid after taking it off at 140°F (60°C) carries it there. Use a thermometer to check.
The mayonnaise uses a raw yolk: use a pasteurised egg for vulnerable guests, keep the dish chilled and eat within 2 days.
Cool the meat and liquid to fridge temperature within 2 hours.
