title: Shrimp Rémoulade
summary: Gulf shrimp boiled in a spicy seasoned crab boil, chilled and served on shredded lettuce with a Creole mustard rémoulade. It is here because it teaches the New Orleans seafood boil, cooking shrimp by steeping rather than boiling hard, and the sharp mustard style of rémoulade that is nothing like the French one.
skills: boiling shrimp in a seasoned crab boil

ingredients.item: Large shrimp, shell on, head off
Liquid or dry crab boil seasoning
Spring onion and flat-leaf parsley, finely chopped

mise: Make the rémoulade first so it has time to chill: whisk everything from the mustard to the parsley with the hot sauce. Taste and chill at least 1 hour.
Fill a large bowl with iced water.
Shred the lettuce very finely and keep it cold.

timeline.do: Make and chill the rémoulade.
Bring the boil to a rolling boil, 10 minutes of seasoning.
Cook the shrimp and shock in iced water.
Peel and devein.
Toss in rémoulade.
Serve on shredded lettuce.

steps.do: Bring the 4 quarts (4 litres) water to the boil with the crab boil, squeezed lemons and their halves, bay and salt. Boil 10 minutes.
steps.look: A rolling boil smelling strongly of spice and lemon; the water tastes like well seasoned sea water.
steps.mistake: Adding the shrimp straight away, before the seasoning has infused.
steps.fix: Let it boil the full 10 minutes.

steps.do: Add the shrimp, stir, and as soon as the water returns to a simmer, turn off the heat. Leave them to steep for 2 to 4 minutes.
steps.look: Shells turn pink, the flesh turns opaque all the way through and the shrimp curl into a loose C shape. A thick one reads 145°F (63°C).
steps.mistake: Boiling them hard, which makes them rubbery and curls them into a tight O.
steps.fix: Check one after 2 minutes; take them out the moment the centre is opaque.

steps.do: Lift the shrimp into the iced water and stir until cold, about 5 minutes. Drain.
steps.look: Firm, cold, glossy pink shrimp.
steps.mistake: Leaving them to cool in the hot liquid, which overcooks them.
steps.fix: Ice water at once; the seasoning has already gone in.

steps.do: Peel the shrimp, leaving the tail on if you like, and devein: run the paring knife shallowly down the back and lift out the dark vein.
steps.look: Clean, pink shrimp with a shallow groove down the back.
steps.mistake: Cutting too deep, which splits the shrimp in two.
steps.fix: A shallow cut is enough; the vein lifts out with the knife tip.

steps.do: Toss the shrimp with about two thirds of the rémoulade.
steps.look: Each shrimp coated in a pinkish-orange, speckled sauce.
steps.mistake: Drowning them in sauce.
steps.fix: Use enough to coat; offer the rest on the side.

steps.do: Pile shredded lettuce on chilled plates and set the shrimp on top. Serve at once with lemon wedges.
steps.look: Cold, crisp lettuce under glossy, sauced shrimp.
steps.mistake: Dressing the lettuce, which wilts it.
steps.fix: Keep the lettuce plain; the sauce runs down into it as you eat.

science: The seafood boil seasons by diffusion: in strongly salted, spiced water, salt and flavour move into the shrimp as they cook. Steeping off the heat cooks them gently, because shrimp protein sets quickly between about 120 and 145°F (49 and 63°C). Boiling hard pushes the outside far past that range before the middle is done, squeezing out moisture and turning the flesh rubbery. Shocking in iced water stops carry-over cooking straight away. Creole rémoulade depends on mustard and horseradish, whose sharp compounds are released when they are ground and mixed with liquid. Chilling the sauce for an hour lets those flavours meld into the mayonnaise base.
plating: A chilled glass or plate: a bed of finely shredded iceberg, the shrimp piled high in the centre, extra rémoulade in a small ramekin, lemon wedge and a sprinkle of chopped spring onion. For a party, stand the shrimp round the rim of a coupe.

pairing.drink: A crisp, dry Riesling or a light lager; the acidity and a touch of fruit calm the spice.
pairing.brennans: New Orleans Shrimp & Grits: Brennan's hot Gulf shrimp dish, a useful comparison for a guest choosing between shrimp served cold and warm.

variations: White rémoulade: a mayonnaise base with Creole mustard, capers and pickles, the other New Orleans style.
Serve on fried green tomatoes for a classic Creole starter.
Use crab claws in place of shrimp.
safety: Cook shrimp until the flesh is opaque throughout, 145°F (63°C), and chill them at once; keep them below 40°F (4°C) until served.
Lift shrimp out of boiling water with a spider; pour the boil away from you into the sink.

title: Chicken Shawarma with Toum
summary: Chicken thighs marinated in yoghurt, lemon and warm spices, roasted until charred at the edges, sliced and re-crisped, wrapped in flatbread with toum, the Lebanese garlic sauce. It is here because toum is an emulsion held by garlic alone, with no egg at all, which makes it the most demanding test yet of slow oil addition.
skills: toum, a garlic emulsion with no egg
equipment: Large mixing bowl or zip bag
Large rimmed baking tray and a wire rack to fit

ingredients.item: Peeled garlic cloves, for the toum
Neutral oil, such as sunflower, for the toum
ingredients.note: not olive oil, which turns bitter

ingredients.item: Pickled turnips, gherkins, tomato and parsley

mise: Halve each garlic clove for the toum and pick out any green shoot.
Measure the oil into a jug with a spout; chill the lemon juice.
Mix all the marinade ingredients in the bowl.

timeline.do: Marinate the chicken (1 to 24 hours).
Make the toum.
Heat the oven to 450°F (230°C).
Roast the chicken.
Rest, slice and re-crisp under the overhead grill (broiler).
Wrap with toum and pickles.

steps.do: Toss the chicken in the marinade until coated and refrigerate at least 1 hour and up to 24.
steps.look: Every piece stained orange-yellow.
steps.mistake: Marinating longer than a day, which makes the surface mushy from the acid.
steps.fix: Keep it to 24 hours at most.

steps.do: Make the toum. Process the garlic and salt in the food processor for 1 minute, scraping down, until finely minced.
steps.look: A sticky, finely chopped paste clinging to the sides.
steps.mistake: Starting the oil before the garlic is properly broken down.
steps.fix: Scrape and process again until it looks like a paste.

steps.do: With the motor running, add oil drop by drop through the feed tube, about 1 tbsp (15 ml) over a full minute.
steps.look: The garlic turns fluffy and pale as it absorbs the first oil.
steps.mistake: Pouring the oil faster at this stage, which breaks the emulsion at once.
steps.fix: Go painfully slowly; this first minute decides success.

steps.do: Continue adding oil in a very thin stream, alternating every 1/4 cup (60 ml) with 1 tbsp (15 ml) of lemon juice and ending with the iced water, for about 10 to 15 minutes in total.
steps.look: A thick, snow-white, fluffy sauce like whipped mayonnaise, that holds stiff peaks.
steps.mistake: The sauce suddenly turns thin and oily: it has split.
steps.fix: Stop. Put 1 tbsp (15 ml) of the broken sauce aside, process an egg white or a fresh clove of garlic with 1 tbsp (15 ml) lemon juice, then add the broken sauce very slowly.

steps.do: Heat the oven to 450°F (230°C). Spread the chicken on the rack over the tray and roast 25 to 30 minutes.
steps.look: Sizzling chicken charred in patches at the edges, 175°F (79°C) at the thickest point.
steps.mistake: Crowding the tray, so the chicken steams pale.
steps.fix: Use two trays if needed; space the pieces apart.

steps.do: Rest 5 minutes, then slice thinly across. Return the slices to the tray, toss in the juices and grill on high for 2 to 3 minutes until the edges crisp.
steps.look: Thin, glistening strips with crisp, dark edges.
steps.mistake: Skipping the re-crisp, so it tastes like roast chicken, not shawarma.
steps.fix: This step mimics the crisp carved surface of a spit.

steps.do: Warm the flatbreads, spread with a generous spoon of toum, add the chicken, pickles, tomato and parsley and roll tightly.
steps.look: A tight wrap, the white garlic sauce visible at the edges.
steps.mistake: Overfilling, so the wrap bursts.
steps.fix: A modest line of filling along one side, then roll firmly.

science: Toum is an emulsion with no egg. Crushing garlic breaks its cells and releases sticky compounds, proteins and fine particles that can coat oil droplets and keep them apart, just as yolk does in mayonnaise, but far less powerfully. That is why the oil must go in drop by drop at first: the garlic can stabilise only a tiny amount of oil at a time until the emulsion has formed. Lemon juice and iced water supply the water phase that lets more droplets fit, and cold helps keep the fat firm. Olive oil is avoided because high-speed blending can release bitter compounds from it. On the chicken, yoghurt's proteins and sugars brown quickly in high heat, giving char.
plating: Wrap each shawarma tightly in baking paper or foil, twisting the base, and cut in half on the diagonal. Or serve as a plate: sliced chicken on a warm platter, toum in a bowl, pickled turnips, tomato, parsley and warm bread alongside.

pairing.drink: A cold mint lemonade, or a Lebanese red from the Bekaa Valley, fruity and spiced to match the warm marinade.
pairing.brennans: Château Musar Bekaa Valley 2003: the celebrated Lebanese red on Brennan's list, from the country whose garlic sauce is the heart of this dish.

variations: Beef shawarma: thinly sliced sirloin with a spice mix heavier on black pepper and cloves.
Serve as a rice bowl with tabbouleh and toum.
Halve the toum recipe and keep it in the fridge for up to 2 weeks for roast potatoes or grilled fish.
safety: Cook chicken thighs to at least 165°F (74°C); 175°F (79°C) makes them more tender.
Wash hands, boards and knives after handling raw chicken, and never put cooked chicken back on the tray that held it raw.
Garlic in oil can support botulism if left warm: keep toum in the fridge and use within 2 weeks.

title: Ceviche Clásico
summary: Peru's ceviche: impeccably fresh white fish cut into cubes and dressed for just a few minutes in leche de tigre, a sharp, spicy lime marinade, with red onion, chilli and coriander, served with sweet potato and corn. It is here because it teaches choosing, skinning and cutting fish to serve raw, and the food safety of raw fish, where freshness and handling are everything.
equipment: Flexible filleting knife and a sharp chef's knife
Glass or stainless steel bowls set over ice
Small saucepan for the sweet potato and corn

ingredients.item: Very fresh firm white fish fillet, skinned
ingredients.note: sea bass, flounder or halibut sold for eating raw, previously frozen
squeezed at the last minute, about 2/3 cup (160 ml)

ingredients.item: Ají limo, ají amarillo or habanero, finely chopped

ingredients.note: peeled and cut into thick slices

ingredients.item: Corn on the cob or choclo

mise: Chill the serving bowls and a mixing bowl set over ice.
Boil the sweet potato and corn in salted water until tender, about 15 minutes, then cool.
Shave the onion paper thin and soak in iced water for 10 minutes, then drain.
Chop the chilli and coriander.
Keep the fish in the coldest part of the fridge until the moment you cut it.

timeline.do: Boil sweet potato and corn; chill the bowls.
Skin, trim and cube the fish; keep it on ice.
Make the leche de tigre.
Salt the fish, add the leche de tigre.
Fold in onion, chilli and coriander.
Serve at once.

steps.do: Check the fish: it should smell of clean sea water, never fishy, with firm, glossy, translucent flesh that springs back when pressed.
steps.look: Bright, firm flesh with no dull or brown patches.
steps.mistake: Using fish that smells sour or feels soft; acid will not fix it.
steps.fix: If in doubt, do not serve it raw; cook it instead.

steps.do: If the fillet has skin, lay it skin side down, hold the tail end and slide the filleting knife between skin and flesh, angled slightly down, pulling the skin back and forth as you push. Pull any pin bones and trim off the dark bloodline.
steps.look: A clean, white fillet with no skin, bones or dark flesh.
steps.mistake: Leaving the dark bloodline, which tastes strong and spoils first.
steps.fix: Cut it away in a shallow V.

steps.do: Cut the fish into even 3/4 inch (2 cm) cubes. Put them in the chilled bowl over ice and return to the fridge.
steps.look: Neat, matching cubes with clean faces.
steps.mistake: Uneven pieces, so small ones cook through in the acid while large ones stay raw.
steps.fix: Cut first into strips, then across into cubes.

steps.do: Make the leche de tigre: blend the lime juice with the garlic, ginger, celery, 2 or 3 small fish trimmings, a few coriander stems, a pinch of chilli, a pinch of salt and the ice for 20 seconds. Strain through the sieve.
steps.look: A cloudy, very cold, sharp and spicy liquid.
steps.mistake: Blending too long, which makes the lime juice bitter.
steps.fix: Twenty seconds is enough; squeeze limes gently, without twisting out the pith.

steps.do: Sprinkle the fish with the salt and toss. Leave 1 minute.
steps.look: The surface of the fish becomes slightly tacky.
steps.mistake: Skipping the salt, so the fish tastes flat.
steps.fix: Salt first; it seasons and firms the flesh.

steps.do: Pour the leche de tigre over the fish and toss gently. Leave 2 to 5 minutes, no longer.
steps.look: The edges of each cube turn milky white and opaque while the centres stay translucent.
steps.mistake: Leaving it for an hour, which turns the fish chalky and dry.
steps.fix: Taste a piece at 2 minutes; serve when the outside is just white.

steps.do: Fold in the drained onion, chilli and chopped coriander. Taste and add salt or lime.
steps.look: Bright, sharp, spicy and cold, the fish silky inside.
steps.mistake: Under-seasoning; ceviche must be bold.
steps.fix: Adjust salt and chilli to taste.

steps.do: Spoon into the chilled bowls with plenty of liquid, and serve at once with sweet potato, corn and cancha.
steps.look: Glistening white fish in a pool of milky leche de tigre, purple onion on top.
steps.mistake: Letting it sit before serving.
steps.fix: Ceviche is made to order; serve within minutes.

science: Lime juice does not cook fish with heat, but its acid changes the proteins on the surface in a similar way. The acid unfolds the proteins, a process called denaturation, and they bond into a firmer, opaque network, which is why the edges turn white. Left too long, the acid works through the whole cube and the texture becomes chalky. Salt draws out a little moisture and also helps the proteins firm. Crucially, the acid does not reliably kill bacteria or parasites, which is why freshness, previously frozen fish and cold handling matter so much. Blending fish trimmings into the leche de tigre adds savoury depth, and keeping everything ice cold keeps the fish firm and safe.
plating: Chilled shallow bowls. Mound the fish in the centre, pour the leche de tigre round it, pile the onion on top with a few coriander sprigs, and set a slice of sweet potato and a round of corn on one side with a small heap of cancha.

pairing.drink: A pisco sour, or a crisp, high-acid white such as Albariño whose citrus and salinity echo the lime.
pairing.brennans: Pazo das Bruxas Albariño 2025: a bright Spanish Albariño from the Brennan's list, the classic white for raw fish and citrus.

variations: Ceviche mixto: add cooked octopus, squid and prawns.
Tiradito: slice the fish thin like sashimi and spoon the leche de tigre over at the last moment.
Use ají amarillo paste in the leche de tigre for a yellow, fruitier version.
safety: Acid does not make fish safe like cooking does. Use fish sold for eating raw and frozen to -4°F (-20°C) for at least 7 days before use, keep it below 40°F (4°C) and serve within minutes of mixing.
Pregnant guests, the very young, the elderly and anyone with a weakened immune system should not eat raw fish.
Use a separate board and knife for raw fish and wash them in hot soapy water afterwards.

title: Pulpo a la Gallega
summary: Galician octopus: a whole octopus tenderised by freezing, dipped three times and simmered until just tender, then cut with scissors over potatoes cooked in its water and dressed with coarse salt, pimentón and olive oil. It is here because octopus is either tender or rubbery with very little in between, and learning to judge that point by touch is the lesson.
equipment: Large deep pot, at least 8 quarts (8 litres)
Long tongs or a large meat fork
Paring knife or a thin skewer

ingredients.note: frozen and thawed in the fridge, or bought frozen
peeled, in 3/4 inch (2 cm) thick slices

ingredients.item: Coarse sea salt or flaky salt

mise: Thaw the octopus in the fridge for 24 hours on a tray.
Rinse it well inside and out under cold water, checking the head is cleaned and the beak removed.
Peel and slice the potatoes.
Warm the plates or board.

timeline.do: Thaw the octopus in the fridge.
Bring the large pot of water to the boil.
Dip the octopus three times, then simmer.
Test for tenderness, rest the octopus in its water.
Cook the potatoes in the octopus water.
Cut, season and serve warm.

steps.do: Bring the large pot of unsalted water to a full boil with the bay and onion.
steps.look: A rolling boil with room for the octopus.
steps.mistake: Salting the water, which some cooks say toughens the skin; salt at the end instead.
steps.fix: Season after cooking with coarse salt.

steps.do: Holding the octopus by the head with tongs, dip it into the boiling water for 3 seconds and lift it out. Repeat twice more.
steps.look: The tentacles curl up tightly into neat spirals each time.
steps.mistake: Dropping it straight in, so the tentacles cook straight and the skin may tear.
steps.fix: Three short dips set the skin and curl the tentacles; it is the Galician way.

steps.do: Lower the octopus in fully, bring back to a simmer and cook at a gentle simmer for 40 to 60 minutes, roughly 20 minutes per lb (450 g).
steps.look: A gentle, steady simmer; the water turns pink and purple.
steps.mistake: A hard rolling boil, which tears the skin off the tentacles.
steps.fix: Turn it down until bubbles only break at the edges.

steps.do: Test the thickest part of a tentacle, where it meets the head, with the paring knife.
steps.look: The knife slides in with slight resistance, like a ripe potato that is not yet soft.
steps.mistake: Taking it out while the knife bounces off, which is rubbery, or leaving it until it falls apart, which is mushy.
steps.fix: Test every 5 minutes after 35 minutes. It goes from firm to tender quickly.

steps.do: Turn off the heat and leave the octopus in its water for 15 minutes.
steps.look: The skin settles and the flesh relaxes and stays moist.
steps.mistake: Lifting it straight out, so the skin wrinkles and slips off.
steps.fix: The rest keeps the skin attached and the texture even.

steps.do: Lift out the octopus and keep it warm on a plate covered with foil. Bring the water back to the boil and cook the potato slices in it for 12 to 15 minutes until tender.
steps.look: Potatoes tinged lilac by the octopus water, tender to the point of a knife.
steps.mistake: Over-boiling the potatoes until they break up.
steps.fix: Check after 10 minutes; drain as soon as tender.

steps.do: Arrange the warm potatoes on the board. Using the scissors, cut the tentacles across into slices 1/2 inch (1 cm) thick, letting them fall over the potatoes. Cut the head into strips.
steps.look: Neat rounds of white flesh edged with purple skin and suckers.
steps.mistake: Cutting with a blunt knife, which drags and tears the skin.
steps.fix: Scissors give clean cuts and are the traditional tool.

steps.do: Scatter the coarse salt, dust generously with sweet and hot pimentón and pour the olive oil over. Serve warm with toothpicks and bread.
steps.look: Rust-red dusting, glistening oil and crunchy salt crystals.
steps.mistake: Using fine table salt, which disappears.
steps.fix: Use flakes or coarse salt for crunch and bursts of seasoning.

science: Octopus is almost all muscle bound with a great deal of collagen, the connective protein that makes it tough. Freezing helps because ice crystals forming inside the flesh break some of the muscle fibres and connective tissue. During cooking there are two phases: first the muscle proteins tighten and squeeze out water, which makes octopus rubbery after a short cook; then, with longer gentle heat, collagen slowly melts into gelatin and the flesh turns tender. That is why there is a narrow window between rubbery and mushy. A gentle simmer converts collagen without tearing the delicate skin, and resting in the hot water lets the gelatin settle so the meat stays moist.
plating: Serve on a round wooden board, the Galician tradition: potatoes overlapping in a single layer, octopus rounds scattered across, a heavy dusting of pimentón and a final drizzle of oil. Toothpicks stuck in a few pieces and crusty bread on the side.

pairing.drink: A crisp Albariño or Godello from northwest Spain, or a light, chilled Mencía red.
pairing.brennans: Raúl Pérez ‘Ultreia’ Godello Bierzo 2021: a Godello from Bierzo, next door to Galicia, on the Brennan's list, the natural white for this dish.

variations: Grilled octopus: after simmering, char the tentacles on a very hot grill and serve with lemon and oregano.
Use pressure-cooked octopus, about 15 minutes at high pressure, for a faster, reliable result.
Serve as tapas on toothpicks without the potatoes.
safety: Thaw frozen octopus in the fridge, never at room temperature.
Lower the octopus into boiling water with long tongs, away from your body.

title: Fiskekaker (Norwegian Fish Cakes)
summary: Norwegian fish cakes made from a fine farce of raw white fish worked with salt until sticky, then bound with starch and cold milk and fried gently in butter. It is here because it introduces the farce, the smooth fish forcemeat behind mousselines and quenelles, and shows how salt and cold make it bind.
skills: a fine fish farce bound with cream and starch
equipment: Large nonstick or heavy frying pan
Two dessert spoons and a glass of cold water

ingredients.item: Skinless white fish fillet, such as haddock, cod or pollock
ingredients.note: very cold, in 1 inch (2.5 cm) pieces

ingredients.item: Whole milk or single cream, ice cold
Unsalted butter and neutral oil, for frying
Carrots, coarsely grated, with lemon and a little sugar

mise: If your fish has skin and bones, skin it (as for ceviche) and pull out every pin bone with tweezers; feel twice.
Cut into pieces and put in the freezer for 15 minutes with the processor bowl and blade.
Chill the milk until ice cold.
Boil the potatoes and make the carrot salad.

timeline.do: Skin, bone and chill the fish; boil potatoes.
Make the farce.
Rest the farce in the fridge.
Shape and fry in two batches.
Serve hot with potatoes and carrot salad.

steps.do: Process the cold fish with the salt for 1 to 2 minutes, scraping down twice.
steps.look: The fish breaks down and then suddenly turns sticky, smooth and pale, clinging to the blade like dough.
steps.mistake: Adding liquid before the fish is sticky, so the farce never binds.
steps.fix: Keep processing with salt alone until it is truly sticky.

steps.do: Add the starch, nutmeg and pepper and pulse to combine.
steps.look: A thick, smooth, glossy paste.
steps.mistake: Overheating the farce by processing too long, which can make it split.
steps.fix: Pulse in short bursts and keep everything cold.

steps.do: With the motor running, pour in the cold milk a little at a time, letting each addition absorb before the next. Stop when the farce is soft but holds its shape on a spoon.
steps.look: A smooth, light, pale paste, like a soft mousse, that holds a peak.
steps.mistake: Adding all the milk at once, so the farce turns loose and cannot be shaped.
steps.fix: Stop adding milk earlier next time; firm it up now by chilling 30 minutes.

steps.do: Scrape into the bowl over ice, fold in the chives and chill 15 minutes. Fry a small test cake for 1 minute a side and taste for salt.
steps.look: The test cake holds together and is springy, tender and well seasoned.
steps.mistake: Not testing, so the whole batch ends up bland or salty.
steps.fix: Adjust the salt now while you can.

steps.do: Heat half the butter and oil in the pan over medium heat until the butter foams. Dip a spoon in cold water, scoop a heaped spoonful of farce, smooth it with the second wet spoon and slide it into the pan. Flatten gently to a cake 1/2 inch (1.5 cm) thick.
steps.look: Neat oval cakes that sizzle gently as they go in.
steps.mistake: A pan too hot, which browns the outside before the middle sets.
steps.fix: Medium heat; they should sizzle softly, not spit.

steps.do: Fry 3 to 4 minutes a side until golden and springy. Check one: the centre should reach 145°F (63°C).
steps.look: Golden brown on both sides; they puff slightly and spring back when pressed.
steps.mistake: Turning them too early, so they break.
steps.fix: Wait until the edges look set and the base is golden before turning.

steps.do: Drain briefly on kitchen paper and fry the second batch with the rest of the fat.
steps.look: A stack of golden, puffed fish cakes.
steps.mistake: Letting the first batch go cold.
steps.fix: Keep them warm in a low oven at 200°F (95°C).

steps.do: Serve with boiled potatoes, the carrot salad and melted butter or a light white sauce.
steps.look: Pale, tender, bouncy cakes with a golden crust.
steps.mistake: Serving with heavy sauce that hides the delicate fish.
steps.fix: Melted butter with chives is all it needs.

science: A farce works like a sausage made from fish. Salt dissolves some of the fish's muscle proteins, mainly myosin, which then become sticky and form a gel that holds water and fat. That is why the fish must be processed with salt first, until it turns sticky, before any liquid goes in. Cold is essential: fish proteins are delicate and start to set or split if they warm up from the friction of the blade. Starch absorbs extra liquid and makes the gel more forgiving. When the cakes are fried, the protein gel sets into a springy, tender texture and traps the milk, which is why good fish cakes are light and bouncy rather than crumbly.
plating: Warm plates: three fish cakes overlapping in a fan, a pile of boiled potatoes dressed in butter and dill beside them, a neat mound of carrot salad, and melted chive butter spooned over the cakes.

pairing.drink: A crisp Muscadet or a dry Riesling, or a cold Norwegian pilsner.

variations: Quenelles: poach spoonfuls of the farce, made with cream and egg white, in barely simmering stock.
Add finely chopped smoked salmon to the farce for a smoky flavour.
Serve in a bun with remoulade as a fish cake burger.
safety: Cook fish cakes until the centre reaches 145°F (63°C).
Keep raw fish and the farce cold, below 40°F (4°C), until cooking.
Check carefully for bones; a farce hides them.

title: Sushi: Hosomaki, Uramaki and Nigiri
summary: Sushi made at home: properly washed and seasoned rice, thin rolls with the nori outside, inside-out rolls with sesame, and nigiri topped with slices of raw fish. It is here because sushi demands perfect rice and confident fish cutting, the two skills that take years to master, and the strictest handling of raw fish in the course.
equipment: Heavy saucepan with a tight lid or a rice cooker
Wide wooden tub (hangiri) or a large wide bowl
Rice paddle or flat wooden spoon
Bamboo rolling mat (makisu), wrapped in cling film for inside-out rolls
Long, very sharp knife (a yanagiba if you have one)
Small bowl of hand water with a splash of vinegar (tezu)
Board kept only for raw fish

ingredients.item: Cold water, for cooking the rice

ingredients.note: sold for eating raw, previously frozen, in a neat block
sold for eating raw, previously frozen
seeds removed, cut into thin batons

ingredients.item: Wasabi, pickled ginger and soy sauce

mise: Wash the rice: cover with cold water, swirl with your hand and drain; repeat four or five times until the water is only faintly cloudy. Drain in the sieve for 30 minutes.
Warm the vinegar, sugar and salt in a small pan just until dissolved, then cool.
Cut the nori sheets in half, cucumber into batons, avocado into slices.
Keep the fish in the coldest part of the fridge until you cut it.
Set up the rolling station: mat, damp cloth, hand water, rice, fillings, knife.

timeline.do: Wash and drain the rice.
Cook the rice, rest it, then season and cool to body temperature.
Slice the fish.
Roll hosomaki and uramaki.
Shape nigiri.
Cut the rolls and serve with wasabi, ginger and soy.

steps.do: Put the drained rice in the pan with the water and kombu. Bring to the boil over medium-high heat, remove the kombu, cover, turn to the lowest heat and cook 12 minutes. Turn off the heat and leave covered 10 minutes.
steps.look: Plump, glossy grains with small steam holes across a flat surface.
steps.mistake: Lifting the lid during cooking, which leaves hard, uneven rice.
steps.fix: Keep the lid on. If the top is firm, sprinkle 1 tbsp (15 ml) water, cover and rest 5 minutes more.

steps.do: Tip the hot rice into the wide tub. Pour the seasoning over the back of the paddle so it spreads out. Cut through the rice at an angle with the edge of the paddle, folding rather than stirring, while fanning it, for about 5 minutes.
steps.look: Each grain glossy and separate; the rice steams off and smells gently sweet and sour.
steps.mistake: Stirring and mashing, which crushes the grains into paste.
steps.fix: Use slicing motions with the paddle edge; fan with a magazine or a fan.

steps.do: Stop when the rice reaches body temperature, about 98°F (37°C). Cover with the damp cloth and use within 2 hours; do not refrigerate.
steps.look: A squeezed handful holds together and the grains are still distinct.
steps.mistake: Chilling it, which turns the rice hard and chalky.
steps.fix: Keep it covered at room temperature and make the sushi the same day.

steps.do: Slice the fish for nigiri. Cut the block across the grain at a slight angle into slices about 3 inches (7.5 cm) long, 1 inch (2.5 cm) wide and 1/4 inch (6 mm) thick. Draw the knife towards you in one long stroke, using the full length of the blade. Cut a few thin strips for the rolls.
steps.look: Glossy slices with smooth faces and clean edges.
steps.mistake: Sawing back and forth, which tears and bruises the flesh.
steps.fix: One pull per slice, heel to tip. Wipe the blade with a damp cloth between cuts.

steps.do: Hosomaki: lay half a nori sheet shiny side down on the mat. Wet your hands in the hand water, take about 3/4 cup (about 100 g) rice and spread it evenly over the nori, leaving a 1/2 inch (1 cm) strip bare at the far edge. Lay a thin line of tuna or cucumber across the middle.
steps.look: A thin, even layer of rice, nori visible through it in places.
steps.mistake: Pressing rice down hard, which makes a dense roll.
steps.fix: Spread with fingertips, pressing lightly.

steps.do: Lift the near edge of the mat, roll it over the filling so the rice edge meets the far rice edge, press gently along the length, then roll forward to seal on the bare strip.
steps.look: A tight, square-ish roll with the seam underneath.
steps.mistake: Rolling the mat into the roll.
steps.fix: Hold the mat's edge up and away as you roll forward.

steps.do: Uramaki: cover the mat with cling film. Spread rice over a half sheet of nori to all edges, sprinkle with sesame, flip it over so the nori is on top, lay salmon, avocado and cucumber along the middle and roll the same way.
steps.look: An inside-out roll, rice and sesame outside.
steps.mistake: Overfilling, so the roll will not close.
steps.fix: Use about half the filling you think.

steps.do: Nigiri: wet your hands, take about 1 tbsp (15 to 20 g) rice and gently shape it into an oval in your palm with two fingers. Dab a little wasabi on a slice of fish, lay the rice on it and press lightly to shape so the fish drapes over.
steps.look: A neat, compact oval of rice holding together, the fish draped smoothly over it.
steps.mistake: Squeezing the rice hard, which makes it dense and gummy.
steps.fix: Gentle pressure; nigiri should hold when lifted but break apart in the mouth.

steps.do: Cut each roll with a wet, sharp knife: hosomaki into 6 pieces, uramaki into 8. Wipe the blade between cuts.
steps.look: Clean cut faces showing a neat circle of filling.
steps.mistake: A dry or blunt knife that squashes the roll.
steps.fix: Wet the blade each time and cut with one long stroke.

science: Washing removes loose surface starch, so the cooked grains stay separate and glossy rather than gummy. Short grain rice is high in amylopectin, the branched starch that makes grains sticky enough to hold together. Seasoning the rice while it is hot works because the swollen, open starch on each grain absorbs the vinegar mixture. Fanning drives off steam so the surface glosses instead of turning wet. Refrigerating cooked rice makes the starch recrystallise and harden, a process called retrogradation. Sushi rice is acidified by the vinegar, which helps it hold more safely at room temperature for a short time. For fish, freezing to a low temperature beforehand kills parasites, and keeping it very cold slows bacteria.
plating: A long wooden board or plain plate: nigiri in pairs in a neat row, the cut rolls standing on their sides to show the filling, a mound of pickled ginger at one corner, a small dot of wasabi, and soy in small dishes. Leave space between items; sushi is eaten in one bite.

pairing.drink: A cold junmai ginjo sake, or a crisp, mineral white such as Muscadet or Chablis that will not overpower raw fish.
pairing.brennans: Domaine de l’Écu ‘Orthogneiss’ Muscadet Sèvre-et-Maine 2022: a precise, saline Muscadet on the Brennan's list, a classic match for raw fish.

variations: Vegetarian rolls with cucumber, avocado, pickled radish and tamagoyaki.
Temaki: hand rolls of nori cones filled with rice and fish, easiest for a party.
Chirashi: a bowl of sushi rice scattered with sliced fish and vegetables.
safety: Use only fish sold for eating raw that has been frozen to -4°F (-20°C) for at least 7 days. Keep it below 40°F (4°C) until the moment you cut it.
Keep a separate board and knife for raw fish; wash hands often and serve sushi within 2 hours of making.
Pregnant guests, the very young, the elderly and anyone with a weakened immune system should not eat raw fish.
A very sharp knife is safer than a blunt one; cut away from your fingers and curl them in when holding fish.

title: Pork Rillettes
summary: Cubes of pork shoulder and back fat cured overnight, cooked slowly in a little wine until they collapse, shredded into strands, potted and sealed under their own fat. It is here because rillettes are confit made into a spread, the first charcuterie in the course, and teach seasoning for food eaten cold and storing it safely under fat.
skills: slow cooking pork in its own fat
equipment: Two forks or a stand mixer with a paddle
Three or four small sterilised jars or ramekins

ingredients.note: about 1.8% of the meat and fat

ingredients.item: Quatre épices or a pinch each of nutmeg, clove, ginger and pepper

mise: The day before, toss the pork and fat with the salt, pepper and spice, cover and refrigerate overnight.
Sterilise the jars by washing in hot soapy water and drying in an oven at 250°F (120°C) for 15 minutes.
Heat the oven to 265°F (130°C) on the day.

timeline.do: Season the pork and fat.
Into the oven for about 4 hours.
Shred and season.
Pot and seal with fat; chill.
Serve; rillettes improve after a few days.
Take out of the fridge so they soften.

steps.do: Put the seasoned pork and fat into the casserole with the garlic, thyme, bay, wine and water. Cover tightly and cook at 265°F (130°C) for about 4 hours.
steps.look: A gentle bubble when you look in; the kitchen smells of thyme and pork.
steps.mistake: Cooking at a higher heat, which fries the meat and makes it dry and stringy.
steps.fix: Low and slow; check the liquid after 2 hours and add a splash of water if it has nearly gone.

steps.do: Test: press a cube with the back of a spoon.
steps.look: It collapses with no pressure, and clear fat has risen above the juices.
steps.mistake: Taking it out too soon, so it shreds into tough threads.
steps.fix: Give it another 30 to 45 minutes.

steps.do: Lift the meat and fat pieces into a bowl with a slotted spoon. Strain the liquid and let the fat rise; spoon the fat off into a cup and keep the juices separately. Discard thyme stalks and bay.
steps.look: Two layers: golden fat on top, savoury jelly-like juice below.
steps.mistake: Throwing the fat and juices away.
steps.fix: Both go back in; they are the flavour and the texture.

steps.do: Shred the meat with two forks, or in the mixer on its lowest speed for about 1 minute, until it is fine strands.
steps.look: Fluffy, separate strands of meat, not a paste.
steps.mistake: Using a food processor, which turns the meat to a smooth paste.
steps.fix: Forks or the mixer's paddle on low; stop as soon as it is stranded.

steps.do: Beat in enough juice and fat, a spoonful at a time, to make it soft and spreadable. Season, then chill a teaspoonful for 5 minutes and taste it cold.
steps.look: A moist, spreadable mixture; the cold taste is well seasoned.
steps.mistake: Seasoning by tasting it hot, which leads to bland rillettes once cold.
steps.fix: Always taste a chilled spoonful and adjust the salt.

steps.do: Pack into the jars, pressing down firmly with the back of a spoon to remove air pockets. Leave 1/2 inch (1 cm) at the top.
steps.look: Dense, level surfaces with no air holes.
steps.mistake: Leaving air pockets, which turn grey and spoil.
steps.fix: Tap the jars on the worktop and press again.

steps.do: Melt the reserved fat and pour a layer about 1/4 inch (5 mm) thick over each jar to seal. Cover and refrigerate at least 2 days before eating.
steps.look: A smooth white seal of fat on each jar once chilled.
steps.mistake: A thin or patchy seal.
steps.fix: Add more melted fat until the surface is completely covered.

steps.do: Take the rillettes out of the fridge 30 minutes before serving. Spread thickly on toasted bread with cornichons and mustard.
steps.look: Soft, rich, spreadable pork, the strands visible.
steps.mistake: Serving fridge-cold, when the fat is hard and the flavour muted.
steps.fix: Let it come to cool room temperature.

science: Rillettes rely on slow cooking in fat and a little liquid. At a low oven temperature, the collagen in pork shoulder slowly melts into gelatin, so the meat fibres fall apart into strands, while the gentle heat stops the muscle tightening and drying out. Salting the day before seasons the meat right through and draws out some moisture. When the meat is beaten with its fat and juices, the fat coats the fibres and the gelatin from the juices binds everything into a spread. Cold fat dulls our perception of salt, so a seasoning that tastes right hot tastes flat cold. The fat seal keeps air off the surface and slows oxidation and drying, though it does not replace refrigeration.
plating: Serve each guest a small jar or ramekin with its seal of fat removed or left on, alongside toasted country bread, cornichons, pickled onions and a pot of grainy mustard on a board.

pairing.drink: A light, fruity red such as Beaujolais or a Loire Chenin Blanc, whose acidity cuts the richness.
pairing.brennans: Louis Jadot Beaujolais-Villages 2021 (375 ml): a light Gamay on the Brennan's list is exactly the wine a French bistro pours with rillettes.

variations: Duck rillettes: use duck legs and duck fat, the classic of southwest France.
Rillettes de saumon: fold flaked poached salmon with smoked salmon, butter and lemon.
Add a little chopped parsley and shallot when shredding for a fresher spread.
safety: The fat seal does not make rillettes shelf stable: keep them in the fridge below 40°F (4°C) and eat within 2 weeks unopened, or within 1 week once opened.
Cool the cooked meat and pot it within 2 hours of leaving the oven.
Use a clean spoon each time to avoid introducing bacteria.

title: Pastrami on Rye
summary: The New York deli sandwich made from scratch: a brisket flat cured for a week in a brine with curing salt, crusted with black pepper and coriander, smoked, then steamed until tender and sliced thick onto rye with mustard. It is here because it is a full curing project, from measured brine to smoke to steam, and teaches the safe use of curing salt.
skills: a week-long wet cure of brisket with curing salt
equipment: Large food-safe container or a heavy zip bag in a container, big enough to submerge the brisket
Smoker or a kettle barbecue set for indirect heat, or an oven
Wood chunks or chips, such as oak, hickory or cherry
Large pot with a steamer rack and lid

ingredients.note: with a 1/4 inch (6 mm) fat cap
weighed; salt volumes vary by brand

ingredients.item: Prague Powder #1 (pink curing salt, 6.25% sodium nitrite)
ingredients.note: weigh it exactly; never substitute Prague Powder #2

mise: Weigh every brine ingredient on the scale; the curing salt must be exact.

Bring 2 cups (480 ml) of the water to the boil with the salt, sugar, curing salt, pickling spice and garlic, stir until dissolved, then add the rest of the water cold and chill the brine completely below 40°F (4°C).
Trim the brisket so the fat cap is even and remove any hard fat.

timeline.do: Make and chill the brine; submerge the brisket.
Cure in the fridge, turning daily.
Rinse, soak 2 hours, dry, rub.
Smoke to 165°F (74°C) inside, about 5 to 6 hours.
Steam until probe tender, about 2 hours.
Slice thick, build sandwiches.

steps.do: Submerge the brisket in the cold brine in the container, weight it down with a plate so it stays under, cover and refrigerate for 6 to 7 days, turning it once a day.
steps.look: The meat firms and turns from red to a cured dusky pink-grey on the outside.
steps.mistake: Curing a thick piece for too few days, which leaves a grey, uncured centre.
steps.fix: For a 2 inch (5 cm) thick flat, give it the full 7 days.

steps.do: Rinse the brisket under cold water, then soak it in fresh cold water for 2 hours, changing the water once. Fry a small piece to taste for salt.
steps.look: A cured, firm brisket; the tasted piece is seasoned but not harsh.
steps.mistake: Skipping the soak, so the finished pastrami is too salty.
steps.fix: If still salty, soak 1 hour more.

steps.do: Pat completely dry. Mix the cracked pepper, coriander, garlic powder, paprika and mustard seed and press it firmly all over the meat in a thick crust.
steps.look: A thick, even, speckled crust covering every surface.
steps.mistake: Grinding the spices fine, which gives a dusty, bitter crust.
steps.fix: Crack them coarsely in a mortar or with the base of a pan.

steps.do: Set up the smoker or barbecue for indirect heat at 225 to 250°F (107 to 121°C) with wood for smoke. Smoke the brisket fat side up until the centre reaches 165°F (74°C), about 5 to 6 hours.
steps.look: Thin, pale blue smoke; the crust darkens to near black and the meat develops a deep red edge.
steps.mistake: Thick white billowing smoke, which makes the meat bitter.
steps.fix: Let the fire burn cleanly; add small amounts of wood. Without a smoker, roast wrapped in foil at 275°F (135°C) instead.

steps.do: Wrap the brisket tightly in foil. Cool and refrigerate if you are steaming the next day, or go straight on.
steps.look: A firm, dark-crusted, fragrant piece of meat.
steps.mistake: Leaving it out to cool for hours.
steps.fix: Refrigerate within 2 hours of finishing the smoke.

steps.do: Steam the brisket on a rack over simmering water in the covered pot for 1 1/2 to 2 1/2 hours, until the probe slides in like butter, about 203°F (95°C).
steps.look: The fat turns soft and translucent and the meat yields completely to the probe.
steps.mistake: Stopping when it reaches temperature but is still tight.
steps.fix: Tenderness is the test, not the number; keep steaming and test every 20 minutes.

steps.do: Rest 10 minutes, then slice across the grain, about 1/4 inch (6 mm) thick, by hand.
steps.look: Glistening slices with a pink interior, dark crust and a clear smoke ring.
steps.mistake: Slicing with the grain, which gives stringy, chewy pieces.
steps.fix: Find the direction of the fibres and cut across them; turn the brisket as the grain changes.

steps.do: Spread the rye with mustard, pile on the hot pastrami, about 6 oz (170 g) a sandwich, close and cut in half. Serve with a pickle.
steps.look: A tall, steaming sandwich of glossy pastrami.
steps.mistake: Adding mayonnaise or other spreads that drown the meat.
steps.fix: Mustard only; let the meat speak.

science: Curing salt contains a measured amount of sodium nitrite. Nitrite reacts with the meat's myoglobin to fix the pink colour that survives cooking, adds the distinctive cured flavour and, importantly, inhibits the bacteria that cause botulism during long, low smoking. Because nitrite is toxic in excess, it is weighed exactly. The salt and nitrite move into the meat by diffusion, which is why a thick cut needs days. Smoke particles and gases dissolve into the moist surface. Steaming then raises the meat slowly to around 203°F (95°C), where brisket's abundant collagen melts into gelatin and the meat turns tender and juicy. The moist heat also softens the crust and the fat.
plating: Classic deli style: two thick slices of rye stuffed high, cut on the diagonal and turned to show the pink layers, a whole half-sour pickle beside it and a small pot of mustard. A tall stack is the point.

pairing.drink: A cream soda or celery soda in the deli tradition, or a cold lager.

variations: Corned beef: the same cure, then simmer instead of smoking and steaming.
Reuben: pastrami or corned beef with sauerkraut, Swiss cheese and Russian dressing grilled on rye.
Serve thin slices hot with mustard and pickles on a board.
safety: Prague Powder #1 is toxic in excess. Weigh it exactly, never use more than the recipe states, label it clearly and keep it away from table salt and children. Never use Prague Powder #2, which is for long dry cures.
Keep the brine and brisket below 40°F (4°C) for the whole cure, in a food-safe container.
Smoked meat must reach at least 165°F (74°C) during the smoke and be refrigerated within 2 hours if not served.

title: Scotch Eggs
summary: Soft-boiled eggs with jammy yolks wrapped in seasoned sausage meat, crumbed and deep fried until the meat is cooked through and the crust golden. It is here because getting a soft yolk inside fully cooked sausage meat is a lesson in timing two doneness targets at once, and it rehearses peeling, crumbing and frying.
skills: frying to cook the meat through
equipment: Deep heavy pan or deep fryer
Thermometer for the oil, and an instant-read thermometer

ingredients.note: 4 to use and 2 spare in case of peeling accidents
or sausages with the skins removed

ingredients.item: Fresh sage and parsley, finely chopped

mise: Bring a pan of water to a rolling boil and set up a bowl of iced water.
Mix the sausage meat with the herbs, mustard, mace and pepper. Fry a little to check the seasoning. Divide into 4 balls of 85 g and chill.
Set out three dishes: seasoned flour, beaten egg, breadcrumbs.

timeline.do: Season and portion the sausage meat.
Boil, chill and peel the eggs.
Wrap, crumb and chill.
Heat the oil.
Fry; finish in the oven if needed.
Rest 2 minutes, cut and serve.

steps.do: Lower 6 eggs straight from the fridge into the boiling water and cook exactly 6 minutes 30 seconds. Lift them straight into the iced water and leave 10 minutes.
steps.look: Eggs completely cold to the touch after chilling.
steps.mistake: Cooking longer, so the yolk is set by the time the meat is cooked.
steps.fix: Use a timer; the yolk keeps cooking in the fryer.

steps.do: Peel carefully: crack the shell all over on the worktop, then peel under a thin stream of cold water, starting from the wide end where the air pocket is.
steps.look: Smooth, unbroken eggs with soft whites.
steps.mistake: Rushing and tearing the soft white.
steps.fix: Peel slowly under water; use a spare egg if one breaks.

steps.do: Lay a square of cling film on the worktop, put a ball of sausage meat on it, cover with another square and press it into a thin, even round about 5 inches (12 cm) across.
steps.look: An even disc about 1/4 inch (6 mm) thick.
steps.mistake: Uneven thickness, which cooks unevenly.
steps.fix: Press with the base of a flat dish for an even disc.

steps.do: Dust an egg in flour, set it in the centre of the disc and use the cling film to wrap the meat up and round it. Press and smooth to seal, with no gaps. Chill 10 minutes.
steps.look: A smooth, even ball with the egg fully enclosed.
steps.mistake: Gaps in the meat, which split in the fryer.
steps.fix: Smooth over any cracks with damp fingers.

steps.do: Roll each ball in flour, then beaten egg, then crumbs, then egg and crumbs again for a thick crust. Chill until frying.
steps.look: A thick, even coating with no bare patches.
steps.mistake: A single thin coat that splits.
steps.fix: Double-coat; it protects the meat and the yolk.

steps.do: Heat the oil to 340°F (170°C). Lower in two eggs at a time and fry 6 to 7 minutes, turning, until deep golden.
steps.look: A steady fizz, a golden-brown crust and a smell of frying bread.
steps.mistake: Oil too hot, browning the crust before the meat cooks.
steps.fix: Keep it at 340°F (170°C) and adjust the heat between batches.

steps.do: Lift out and check the meat with the instant-read thermometer pushed into the sausage layer, not the egg.
steps.look: The sausage meat reads 160°F (71°C).
steps.mistake: Serving undercooked sausage meat.
steps.fix: If under, finish in an oven at 400°F (200°C) for 3 to 5 minutes.

steps.do: Drain on the rack 2 minutes, then cut in half with a sharp knife and serve.
steps.look: A crisp crust, a ring of browned sausage and a bright, jammy yolk.
steps.mistake: Cutting with a blunt knife, which squashes the yolk out.
steps.fix: Use a serrated or very sharp knife and cut in one stroke.

science: The puzzle is two targets: sausage meat must reach 160°F (71°C), while a jammy yolk sets above roughly 158°F (70°C). The solution is to start with a cold, soft-boiled egg wrapped in a layer of raw meat. Heat moves from the oil inward, so the meat is cooked first and acts as insulation, while the chilled egg begins far colder and lags behind. By the time the meat is done, the yolk has warmed but not set. The crumb coat is a barrier: flour dries the surface, egg glues the crumbs, and the crust browns while protecting the meat from direct contact with the oil. Oil at 340°F (170°C) gives time for the inside to cook before the crust darkens.
plating: Halve each egg and stand the halves cut side up on a board or plate so the yolk glows, with a pot of English mustard or piccalilli and a few dressed leaves. Sprinkle a little flaky salt on the yolks.

pairing.drink: A pint of English bitter or a dry cider, the pub pairing.
pairing.brennans: Housemade Pork Sausage Patty: Brennan's own sausage, a good comparison when explaining how seasoning and fat make a breakfast sausage.

variations: Use black pudding mixed into the sausage meat for a richer flavour.
Quail Scotch eggs: boil quail eggs for 2 minutes 15 seconds for bite-size versions.
Bake at 400°F (200°C) for 20 to 25 minutes instead of frying, for a less crisp version.
safety: Hot oil: fill the pan no more than a third full, lower the eggs in with a spider, and keep a lid nearby. Never use water on burning oil.
Cook sausage meat to 160°F (71°C); check with a thermometer.
Use pasteurised eggs for vulnerable guests, as the yolk stays soft.

title: Chicken Souvlaki with Tzatziki and Pita
summary: Greek chicken skewers made from thighs you bone yourself, cut into even cubes, marinated in lemon, oregano and garlic and grilled over high heat, wrapped in soft homemade pita with tzatziki. It is here because boning thighs and cubing them evenly so every piece cooks at once is basic butchery, and it adds a simple yeasted flatbread.
equipment: Boning knife or small sharp knife
Metal skewers, or wooden ones soaked 30 minutes
Barbecue with hot coals, or a ridged cast-iron grill pan
Box grater and a clean tea towel
Heavy dry frying pan or cast-iron pan

ingredients.note: gives about 1 1/2 lb (680 g) of meat

ingredients.item: Sugar and salt, for the pita
Dill, chopped, red wine vinegar and olive oil
ingredients.metric: about 3 g dill, 15 ml vinegar, 15 ml oil

mise: Make the pita dough: mix flour, yeast, sugar, salt, warm water and oil, knead 5 minutes and leave to rise 1 hour.
Grate the cucumber, toss with a pinch of salt, leave 10 minutes and squeeze dry in the tea towel. Mix with yoghurt, garlic, dill, vinegar and oil; chill.
Soak wooden skewers if using.
Slice tomato and onion.

timeline.do: Make the pita dough and the tzatziki.
Bone and cube the chicken; marinate 2 hours.
Light the coals or heat the grill pan; shape pitas.
Cook the pitas; keep warm in a cloth.
Grill the skewers.
Wrap with tzatziki, tomato and onion.

steps.do: Bone the thighs. Lay a thigh skin side down. Cut along both sides of the bone down its length, then scrape the meat away from the bone with the knife tip, working round it, and cut under the knuckle at each end to free it.
steps.look: A flat piece of thigh with the bone removed cleanly and little meat left on it.
steps.mistake: Hacking at the meat and leaving half of it on the bone.
steps.fix: Keep the knife tip against the bone and use short scraping strokes.

steps.do: Remove the skin if you like and trim away tendons and large pieces of fat. Cut the meat into even 1 1/4 inch (3 cm) cubes.
steps.look: A pile of matching cubes.
steps.mistake: Uneven pieces, so small ones dry out while big ones stay raw.
steps.fix: Cut strips of even width first, then cut across them.

steps.do: Toss the cubes with the oil, lemon, garlic, oregano, honey, salt and pepper. Cover and refrigerate 1 to 4 hours.
steps.look: Glossy cubes flecked with oregano.
steps.mistake: Marinating overnight in lots of lemon, which makes the surface mealy.
steps.fix: Keep it to a few hours.

steps.do: Thread onto skewers, pushing the pieces snugly together without crushing them.
steps.look: Even skewers with pieces touching.
steps.mistake: Packing so tightly the middle stays raw, or spacing so loosely they dry out.
steps.fix: Snug, not squashed.

steps.do: Divide the risen dough into 6, roll each to a round 1/4 inch (6 mm) thick and cook in the very hot dry pan for 1 to 2 minutes a side until puffed and spotted brown. Wrap in a cloth.
steps.look: Soft rounds that puff up and colour in patches.
steps.mistake: Rolling too thin, which makes them crisp rather than soft.
steps.fix: Keep them thicker; wrap at once to keep soft.

steps.do: Grill the skewers over hot coals or in the smoking hot grill pan for 10 to 12 minutes, turning every 2 to 3 minutes, until charred at the edges.
steps.look: Sizzling, golden-brown cubes charred at the corners, smelling of lemon and oregano.
steps.mistake: Moving them constantly, so they never colour.
steps.fix: Leave them still until they release easily, then turn.

steps.do: Check a cube in the middle of a skewer with the thermometer: it should read at least 165°F (74°C), better 175°F (79°C). Rest 3 minutes.
steps.look: Juicy, opaque meat with no pink.
steps.mistake: Serving underdone chicken.
steps.fix: Return to the heat for 2 to 3 minutes more.

steps.do: Spread a warm pita with tzatziki, slide the chicken off the skewer onto it, add tomato and onion, sprinkle oregano and roll.
steps.look: A soft wrap bursting with charred chicken and white tzatziki.
steps.mistake: Overfilling, so it splits.
steps.fix: A modest amount; roll it in paper for eating.

science: Even pieces cook evenly because heat travels inwards at a steady rate, so a cube twice as thick takes much longer to reach temperature. Thigh meat suits grilling because it has more fat and connective tissue than breast, which keeps it juicy at the higher temperatures it can stand. The lemon in the marinade slightly loosens surface proteins and the salt seasons and helps hold moisture. Honey's sugars brown quickly over high heat, giving the charred corners. In the tzatziki, salting the cucumber draws out water by osmosis, so the sauce stays thick. The pita puffs because steam from the dough's water forms a pocket between its two surfaces in a very hot pan.
plating: Wrapped in paper, half peeled back, for a street style plate; or on a platter with the skewers laid over warm pita, a bowl of tzatziki, tomato wedges, sliced red onion, lemon wedges and oregano sprinkled over.

pairing.drink: A crisp Greek Assyrtiko, whose bright lemony acidity mirrors the marinade.
pairing.brennans: Gaia ‘Wild Ferment’ Assyrtiko Santorini 2023: a Santorini Assyrtiko on the Brennan's list, the classic Greek white for grilled chicken.

variations: Pork souvlaki: shoulder cubed the same way, the most common version in Greece.
Serve on a plate with lemon potatoes and Greek salad instead of in pita.
Add red pepper and onion pieces between the chicken.
safety: Cook chicken to at least 165°F (74°C).
Use a separate board and knife for raw chicken, and never use the raw marinade as a sauce.
Boning knives are sharp and narrow: cut away from your holding hand and work slowly.

title: Tacos al Pastor
summary: Mexico City's taco: thin sheets of pork shoulder marinated in a red chilli and achiote adobo, stacked into a home trompo crowned with pineapple, roasted, then carved in thin shavings and crisped onto warm tortillas. It is here because it teaches slicing a shoulder into even sheets and carving from a vertical stack, a butchery and carving lesson in one.
equipment: Large bowl or container for marinating
Loaf tin or small roasting tin, and a long metal skewer or two
Half an onion, for the base of the stack
Large cast-iron frying pan or plancha

ingredients.note: or a pinch of ground clove
a thick slab for the top, the rest in wedges

ingredients.item: White onion and coriander leaves, finely chopped

mise: Toast the chillies in a dry pan for 15 to 20 seconds a side until fragrant, then soak in hot water 20 minutes.
Blend the drained chillies with the achiote, pineapple juice, vinegar, garlic, oregano, cumin, cloves and salt to a smooth, thick paste.
Partly freeze the pork for 1 hour so it is firm to slice.

timeline.do: Slice the pork and marinate overnight.
Heat the oven to 375°F (190°C); build the trompo.
Roast 75 to 90 minutes.
Rest, then carve thin shavings.
Crisp the shavings; warm tortillas; char pineapple.
Build small tacos and eat in twos and threes.

steps.do: Slice the semi-frozen pork against its grain into broad sheets about 1/4 inch (6 mm) thick, working with long, even strokes.
steps.look: Even, wide slices of the same thickness.
steps.mistake: Uneven slices, which cook at different rates in the stack.
steps.fix: Firmer meat slices more evenly; return it to the freezer if it softens.

steps.do: Coat every sheet thoroughly in the adobo, cover and refrigerate overnight.
steps.look: Every surface painted deep brick red.
steps.mistake: Marinating only an hour, which gives a shallow flavour.
steps.fix: At least 6 hours; overnight is best.

steps.do: Build the trompo: stand the half onion cut side down in the loaf tin and push the skewer upright through it. Thread the pork sheets onto the skewer one at a time, pressing each down firmly, turning each sheet a little so the stack is even, until you have a tight, rough cone. Top with the thick pineapple slab.
steps.look: A tall, compact stack, wider at the base, the pineapple on top.
steps.mistake: A loose stack that slumps and cooks unevenly.
steps.fix: Press down firmly after every few sheets; use two skewers if it leans.

steps.do: Roast at 375°F (190°C) for 75 to 90 minutes, until the outside is charred at the edges and the centre reads 175 to 185°F (80 to 85°C).
steps.look: Dark, crisp, caramelised edges and dripping juices; the pineapple caramelises and drips over the pork.
steps.mistake: Pulling it out at 145°F (63°C), when the stacked shoulder is still chewy.
steps.fix: Roast longer; the fat and connective tissue need the extra heat to soften.

steps.do: Rest 10 minutes. Holding the stack upright with tongs, carve thin shavings from the outside downwards with the sharp knife, as a taquero would.
steps.look: Thin, crisp-edged shavings falling away, glistening red.
steps.mistake: Hacking thick chunks, which loses the crisp-edge character.
steps.fix: Carve only the outside layer, then roast the stack 10 minutes more for another crisp round if needed.

steps.do: Crisp the shavings on the hot cast-iron pan with a spoonful of the drippings for 1 to 2 minutes. Char the pineapple wedges in the same pan and chop small.
steps.look: Sizzling, crisp edges and caramelised pineapple.
steps.mistake: Overcrowding the pan, so the meat steams.
steps.fix: Work in batches.

steps.do: Warm the tortillas on a dry hot pan for 30 seconds a side, stack them in the cloth. Use two tortillas per taco if they are thin.
steps.look: Soft, pliable, lightly spotted tortillas.
steps.mistake: Cold, stiff tortillas that crack.
steps.fix: Wrap them warm in a cloth so they steam soft.

steps.do: Top each tortilla with meat, a little pineapple, chopped onion and coriander, and serve with lime wedges and salsa verde.
steps.look: Small, neat tacos: red pork, gold pineapple, white onion, green herbs.
steps.mistake: Overloading, so the taco falls apart.
steps.fix: Small tacos, eaten in two or three bites.

science: Thin sheets in a tight stack behave like the vertical spit: fat renders from the upper layers and bastes those below, while the outside, exposed to dry oven heat, browns and crisps. Achiote's annatto seeds give an earthy flavour and a deep red-orange colour, and the acid in the vinegar and pineapple juice seasons the meat. Fresh pineapple contains bromelain, an enzyme that breaks down proteins, but only juice in moderate amounts is used so the meat does not turn mushy overnight; cooking destroys the enzyme. Shoulder has plenty of fat and collagen, which need a final temperature well above the minimum safe point to soften, which is why the stack is taken to 175 to 185°F (80 to 85°C).
plating: Tacos served on a plate in threes, slightly overlapping, onion and coriander scattered, a lime wedge at the side and salsa in a small bowl. For a party, bring the carved trompo to the table on a board and carve to order.

pairing.drink: A cold Mexican lager with lime, or an agua fresca of pineapple; for wine, an off-dry Riesling handles the chilli and sweetness.

variations: Pan al pastor: sear the marinated sheets hard in a cast-iron pan and chop, for a weeknight.
Gringas: al pastor with melted cheese in a flour tortilla.
Use chicken thighs marinated the same way.
safety: Partially frozen meat slices more easily but is still slippery; use a sharp knife and keep fingers curled.
Pork must reach at least 145°F (63°C) with a rest; this recipe goes higher for tenderness. Use a thermometer.
The skewer and tin are very hot after roasting; use oven gloves and tongs to carve.

title: Bún Chả
summary: Hanoi's lunch: grilled pork patties and caramelised slices of pork belly served in a bowl of warm, balanced dipping sauce, with cold rice vermicelli and a mountain of herbs. It is here because the dipping sauce, nước chấm, must balance salt, sweet, sour and heat by taste alone, and because a caramel marinade teaches grilling sugar without burning it.
equipment: Small heavy saucepan for the caramel
Charcoal grill or a hinged grilling basket, or an oven grill (broiler) with a rack

ingredients.item: Fish sauce, for the nước chấm
Garlic and bird's eye chilli, finely chopped
Green papaya or kohlrabi and carrot, thinly sliced
ingredients.note: quick pickled in a little of the sauce

ingredients.item: Lettuce, perilla, mint, coriander and Thai basil

mise: Make a caramel sauce: melt 2 tbsp (25 g) sugar with 1 tbsp (15 ml) water in the small pan over medium heat, swirling, until deep amber, then carefully add 2 tbsp (30 ml) hot water. It will spit. Cool.
Make the nước chấm: dissolve the sugar in the warm water, add fish sauce and lime, then garlic and chilli. Taste and balance. Add the sliced papaya and carrot.
Pick and wash the herbs.
Chop shallots and garlic.

timeline.do: Make caramel and nước chấm.
Marinate the pork belly and the mince for 1 to 2 hours.
Light the coals or heat the grill; cook noodles.
Shape patties and grill both porks.
Warm the meat in the sauce bowls.
Serve with noodles and herbs.

steps.do: Mix half the shallots and garlic, the fish sauce, 1 tbsp (13 g) sugar, pepper, oil and 1 tbsp (15 ml) caramel. Pour half over the belly slices and mix the other half into the mince. Marinate 1 to 2 hours in the fridge.
steps.look: Glossy, dark-tinted pork smelling of fish sauce and shallot.
steps.mistake: Adding too much caramel, which burns on the grill.
steps.fix: One spoonful in each is enough for colour.

steps.do: Taste the nước chấm with a piece of lettuce. Adjust: more lime if flat, more sugar if harsh, more fish sauce if it tastes weak, more water if strong.
steps.look: A sauce that tastes salty, sweet and sour at once, with chilli heat behind; you should want to drink a spoonful.
steps.mistake: Making it strong like a dip, when it is meant to be a light broth.
steps.fix: Dilute with warm water until you can sip it.

steps.do: Cook the vermicelli in boiling water for 3 to 4 minutes, drain, rinse under cold water and leave to drain in nests.
steps.look: Soft, separate white noodles.
steps.mistake: Leaving them in a wet heap, which sticks together.
steps.fix: Rinse well and twirl into small nests while still damp.

steps.do: Shape the mince into small flat patties about 2 inches (5 cm) across and 1/2 inch (1 cm) thick.
steps.look: Even little patties.
steps.mistake: Big thick patties that char before cooking through.
steps.fix: Small and thin cook quickly and evenly.

steps.do: Grill the belly slices and patties over hot coals or under a hot grill, 3 to 4 minutes a side, turning when charred in places.
steps.look: Caramelised, sticky, charred edges, sizzling fat and a sweet smoky smell.
steps.mistake: Grilling too close to the heat, so the sugar blackens before the pork cooks.
steps.fix: Raise the rack or move to a cooler part of the grill.

steps.do: Check a patty with the thermometer: 160°F (71°C) in the centre.
steps.look: Juicy, cooked through, no pink.
steps.mistake: Serving underdone mince.
steps.fix: Return to the grill for a minute more.

steps.do: Warm the nước chấm gently, divide into four bowls and add the grilled meats to the bowls.
steps.look: Pork pieces bobbing in a warm, amber sauce.
steps.mistake: Boiling the sauce, which dulls the lime.
steps.fix: Just warm it.

steps.do: Serve each person a bowl of pork in sauce, a plate of noodle nests and a shared platter of herbs and lettuce. Dip noodles and herbs into the bowl as you eat.
steps.look: A table of colour: amber sauce, white noodles, green herbs.
steps.mistake: Pouring the sauce over the noodles.
steps.fix: Keep them separate; the eater dips.

science: Caramel adds colour and a bittersweet depth because heating sugar breaks it down into hundreds of new aroma compounds. A little in the marinade helps the pork brown quickly on the grill, but sugar burns fast above about 350°F (175°C), so thin slices, moderate heat and a spoonful only. Fish sauce provides salt and savoury glutamates. Balancing nước chấm is about how tastes interact: sugar softens the perception of sour and salty, acid brightens and lifts salt, and diluting with water makes the sauce light enough to dip noodles in without overpowering. Rinsing the noodles removes surface starch so they do not clump.
plating: Each person gets a small bowl of warm sauce with the pork, a plate of noodle nests and a share of a big herb platter with lettuce leaves, mint, perilla, coriander and basil. Extra chilli and garlic in small dishes. Add fried spring rolls if you are ambitious.

pairing.drink: A cold Vietnamese lager or an off-dry Riesling whose sweetness and acidity match the sauce.
pairing.brennans: C.H. Berres ‘Old Vines’ Riesling 2022: an off-dry Mosel Riesling on the Brennan's list, the classic match for sweet, sour and spicy dishes.

variations: Bún thịt nướng: the same grilled pork served in one bowl over noodles and herbs with the sauce poured over.
Add crisp fried spring rolls (nem rán) cut into pieces.
Use chicken thighs for the patties and slices.
safety: Cook minced pork to 160°F (71°C) and sliced belly until no pink remains.
Caramel is extremely hot and spits when water is added; stand back, add the water slowly and keep children away.
Keep raw pork away from the herbs and cooked noodles.

title: Mul Naengmyeon
summary: Korea's cold noodle soup: chewy buckwheat noodles in an icy, perfectly clear beef broth sharpened with radish water kimchi brine, topped with sliced beef, egg, cucumber and pear. It is here because it demands a broth that is completely clear and fat free when cold, the strictest stock test yet, and noodles rinsed until they squeak.
skills: a clear beef broth chilled and fat removed
equipment: Large container for chilling the broth
Ladle and a spoon for removing fat
Glass jar for the radish brine
Chilled serving bowls, ideally stainless steel

ingredients.note: half in the broth, half for the brine

ingredients.item: Fine salt and sugar, for the radish brine

ingredients.note: for the brine, plus more to serve
half grated for the brine, half sliced to serve

ingredients.item: Korean hot mustard (gyeoja) or English mustard

mise: Make a quick radish brine the day before: slice half the radish thinly, toss with the salt and sugar for 30 minutes, then add 2 cups (480 ml) water, the vinegar, the grated half pear and a slice each of garlic and ginger. Refrigerate.
Soak the beef in cold water for 30 minutes to draw out blood, then drain.
Cut the cucumber into matchsticks and slice the pear just before serving.

timeline.do: Make the radish brine; make the beef broth, strain and chill overnight.
Lift off the fat; season the broth with brine.
Put the broth in the freezer until slushy.
Slice the beef; prepare toppings.
Cook and rinse the noodles.
Assemble the bowls with icy broth.

steps.do: Put the beef, 10 cups (2.4 litres) water, onion, half the radish, garlic, ginger, spring onions and peppercorns in the stockpot. Bring to the boil, skim all the foam, then reduce to a bare simmer and cook 1 1/2 hours.
steps.look: A clear, gently trembling broth, foam skimmed off as it rises.
steps.mistake: Boiling hard, which clouds the broth.
steps.fix: Keep it at a quiver and skim regularly.

steps.do: Lift out the beef when a chopstick slides in easily, wrap it and refrigerate. Strain the broth through the muslin-lined sieve, cool it quickly and refrigerate overnight.
steps.look: A clear golden broth that sets with a layer of fat on top.
steps.mistake: Leaving the broth warm on the worktop for hours.
steps.fix: Cool in a sink of iced water, then refrigerate within 2 hours.

steps.do: Next day, lift off every piece of solid fat with a spoon, then blot the surface with kitchen paper.
steps.look: A completely clear broth with no fat spots.
steps.mistake: Leaving specks of fat, which turn waxy and coat the mouth when cold.
steps.fix: Blot with kitchen paper laid flat on the surface.

steps.do: Mix the broth with about 1 1/2 cups (360 ml) of the strained radish brine. Season with soup soy, sugar, a splash of vinegar and salt. Taste it cold.
steps.look: A clear, cold broth that is savoury, gently sweet and tangy all at once.
steps.mistake: Seasoning warm broth, which tastes too strong; cold dulls flavour, so season cold.
steps.fix: Taste cold and adjust; it should taste lively.

steps.do: Put the broth in the freezer for 1 to 2 hours, stirring once or twice, until icy and slushy at the edges.
steps.look: Thin ice crystals forming, broth very cold.
steps.mistake: Freezing it solid.
steps.fix: Check every 30 minutes; if solid, leave at room temperature to soften.

steps.do: Slice the cold beef very thin across the grain.
steps.look: Thin, neat slices.
steps.mistake: Thick slices that are chewy cold.
steps.fix: Cut thin with a sharp knife.

steps.do: Boil the noodles in plenty of water for 40 to 60 seconds, or as the packet says, stirring. Drain and plunge into iced water, then rub them hard between your hands under cold running water.
steps.look: Noodles turn springy and chewy and lose their surface starch; the water runs clear and they squeak.
steps.mistake: Overcooking, which makes them soft and sticky.
steps.fix: Time it exactly; rinse until they squeak.

steps.do: Twist each portion into a nest in a chilled bowl. Top with beef, half an egg, cucumber and pear. Ladle the icy broth around. Serve with scissors, mustard and vinegar.
steps.look: A clear, icy broth around a tight nest of noodles and neat toppings.
steps.mistake: Leaving noodles in long strands that are hard to eat.
steps.fix: Snip the noodles with scissors at the table.

science: A cold broth reveals every fault. Fat that is invisible in hot soup solidifies when chilled into waxy flecks that coat the tongue, so the broth is chilled overnight to let the fat rise and set into a layer that can be lifted off. Gentle simmering and skimming keep proteins and fat from being churned into suspension, so the broth stays clear. Cold also dulls our ability to taste salt and sweetness, which is why the broth is seasoned cold and more boldly than a hot one. The radish brine adds acidity and a gentle fermented tang. Buckwheat noodles blended with potato or sweet potato starch are very elastic; rinsing removes the surface starch that would make them sticky.
plating: Chilled stainless or glass bowls: a tight nest of noodles centred, beef slices fanned on one side, half an egg on top, cucumber and pear matchsticks beside it, broth poured gently around so the nest stays visible, a few ice crystals floating. Mustard and vinegar on the side.

pairing.drink: Cold barley tea, or a crisp, dry Riesling with plenty of acidity.

variations: Bibim naengmyeon: the same noodles tossed in a spicy sweet gochujang sauce, with a little broth on the side.
Use a light chicken broth instead of beef.
Use store-bought dongchimi brine to save a day.
safety: Cool the broth quickly and refrigerate within 2 hours; keep it cold until serving.
Eat the cooked beef within 3 days of cooking.
